1 Executive summary Revision note. This version incorporates a second adversarial review focused on distribution. Net effect: the addressable market is narrowed to the organised segment (§3) because 75–80% of Indian operators own fewer than five trucks SOURCED ; a channel architecture and a stripped compliance SKU are added (§6); the low-end competitor at ₹4,500–11,000 is named in §7; ASP erosion is flagged against the flat-price assumption in §8; and two risks (11, 12) are added. The FY32 trajectory is unchanged as a target, but it now depends explicitly on OEM line-fit and channel rather than on direct sales into the 5M base. This is the India plan, and it is the funded one. A companion document, BP-1B, covers United States market entry, a different buyer, a different trigger and a different product posture, owned by an incoming co-founder and carrying no revenue forecast. Nothing in this document depends on that one. This document contains two plans, not one. Part A is India: funded, dated, and driven by a compliance mandate. Part B is the United States: a different buyer, a different trigger and a different product posture, owned by an incoming co-founder and deliberately carrying no revenue forecast until a first partner conversation closes. Part C is what they share, one raise, one tapeout, one risk register. Revision note. This version incorporates a five-perspective adversarial review (practitioner, academic, skeptic, economist, historian).

Net effect: OEM/Tier-1 line-fit is demoted from a committed 9–18-month milestone to opportunistic upside (§6); government/defence and insurer-co-funded retrofit are promoted to the primary near-term revenue engine because neither depends on the certification, tapeout, or an OEM relationship DeepGrid does not yet have; a field-support cost reserve (§5) and a tenth risk, incumbent fast-follow by Bosch/ Continental, who already manufacture in India (§7, §10), have been added. chunks.section: Executive summary. DeepGrid Semi sells the certification stamp, not the autonomy
chunks.text: Executive summary. DeepGrid Semi sells the certification stamp, not the autonomy dream. MoRTH GSR 184(E), live April 2026, mandates certified ADAS on every new N2/N3 commercial truck sold in India, a regulatory demand floor across a 5M+ truck base. The AD2 kit prices at ₹2.3L (₹2–2.5L band) PLAN against imports at ₹6.5L (Mobileye EyeQ6) to ₹15L (Nvidia Orin), a ~2.8–6.5× gap ASSUMPTION ARITHMETIC . Owning the compute (28nm die, packaged part ₹1,750 PLAN ) lets us hold that price while gross margin expands from 45% (FPGA phase, FY27) to ~72% in the ASIC phase. Three stacked motions run on one hardware platform: (1) fleet retrofit kits now, no regulatory gate, revenue from day one; (2) OEM/Tier-1 line-fit for the mandate channel, the volume engine, entered after AIS-162/188 certification; (3) private- land driverless at ports, mines and plant yards, sold as per-vehicle-per-month software at 90%+ gross margin. The first retrofit customers are plant operators with private yards: one logo carries the kit sale, the data flywheel, and the future driverless contract. Primary planning numbers, from the working model (Business Plan v2.2): ADAS segment revenue ₹914 Cr at FY32 inside a company total of ₹1,388 Cr, with EBITDA breakeven in FY2028. Traction today: ₹1.01 Cr defence revenue CONTRACTED ; AD0-class perception proven on FPGA (40 fps YOLOv11n MEASURED ). 2 India: market and why now The mandate is the market. GSR 184(E) makes ADAS a compliance requirement rather than a discretionary safety upgrade. Regulation, not persuasion, generates the demand: MARKET FACT VALUE EVIDENCE Mandated N2/N3 truck base 5M+ PLAN, a base, not annual sales ADAS penetration across Indian vehicles today <5% PLAN Road deaths per year, India 1.68 lakh PLAN

MARKET FACT VALUE EVIDENCE, of which ADAS-addressable 60%+ PLAN Kits required to hit the FY32 plan ~49,000 ASSUMPTION arithmetic, as a share of the mandated base <1% ASSUMPTION, no heroic share required Annual N2/N3 sales volume not in source material share-of-annual-sales cannot be computed Why now: OEM design-in awards triggered by the mandate are assumed decided over the next 12–24 months WINDOW LENGTH NOT IN GROUNDING . Atmanirbhar and defence procurement rules exclude foreign silicon from government fleets. The 28nm ASIC tapes out ~Q1–mid 2027 PLAN , collapsing compute COGS ₹65K → ₹1,750 PLAN; RECONCILED IN §5 exactly as line-fit volume arrives. Honest distinction. The mandate covers new truck sales only, OEM fitment, not fleet retrofits. Retrofit is our self-funded bridge to the mandate channel, not the mandate itself. A live mandate with no certified supplier. Mandate in force since April 2026, <5% penetration, our certification a path not a held cert (§10 risk 1), imports not yet AIS-certified ASSUMPTION, §7 : these cannot all hold under full enforcement while new trucks keep selling. The only consistent reading is that enforcement is transitional or phased today NOT IN GROUNDING . Consequence: near-term mandate demand is design-in, not shipped- kit, demand, hence FY27–28 revenue rests on retrofit and government lines, and hence the window: the first supplier certified at Indian prices takes the design-ins before enforcement bites. 3 India: Customer and use cases Customer 1, light-fleet (5t) retrofit operators (now → 9 months, Phase 1). The market structure this plan has to survive An adversarial review of this document found that the buyer described above is real but describes a minority of the Indian market. The structure of Indian trucking is the single most important fact about our distribution problem, and it was previously absent from this plan: MARKET-STRUCTURE FACT VALUE EVIDENCE Trucks on Indian roads 12.5M SOURCED Truck operators 3.5M SOURCED Operators owning fewer than five trucks 75–80% SOURCED Share of India’s freight moved by sub-five-truck operators 85% SOURCED Implied kits per month to hit the FY32 plan 4,000 arithmetic on §8 ASSUMPTION What this does to the buyer definition above. “One signer, no committee” is accurate for an organised fleet and misleading as a description of the market. Most Indian trucks belong to operators with fewer than five vehicles, which means the 5M+ mandated base is not a base we can sell into directly at any realistic cost of acquisition. Two consequences this plan now adopts: our addressable segment is the organised market, defined below; and everything beyond it must be reached through a channel (§6), not a sales force. chunks.section: Second: government/PSU/defence (§3 Customer 2); the GeM record
chunks.text: Second: government/PSU/defence (§3 Customer 2); the GeM record CONTRACTED opens doors. Third, the mandate channel, reframed as upside, not a committed date. OEM/Tier-1 design-in is relationship-gated: comparable regulation-created hardware markets (EU tachograph, eCall) show mandate volume normally flows to whichever supplier already has OEM relationships and homologation experience, not the cheapest new entrant, those incumbents typically absorbed aftermarket share within ~18 months once line-fit normalized EXTERNAL REFERENCE . This plan therefore pursues OEM/Tier-1 engagement opportunistically from month one (a) AIS-162/188 certification (T2-funded, §9) PLAN , (b) retrofit field- hours and Indian-road data as validation, (c) the T2 milestone clock (§9), but does not treat a signed design-in as a required, dated event the way §8's revenue trajectory implicitly assumes. The pitch leads with capability, not price: owning perception + compute + model on Jiyu's <100 ms ASIL-D EHB lets us certify a single photon-to-brake latency number no mix-and-match integration can produce, but that pitch needs an actual OEM contact, which this plan does not yet have (§10 risk 10). Phase-3 expansion: yard-owning retrofit logos convert to driverless pilots under the same single-signer structure, acceptance criteria as moves/day and incidents, then multi-year PVPM contracts; a reusable site playbook cheapens each successive deployment. Channel economics, promoted from footnote to primary near-term engine.

chunks.section: Second: government/PSU/defence (§3 Customer 2); the GeM record
chunks.text: Government/ defence (§3 Customer 2) and insurer-co-funded retrofit are the two revenue lines that do not depend on the AIS-certification clock, the ASIC-tapeout clock, or an OEM relationship DeepGrid does not yet have, they should therefore carry FY27–FY28 revenue, not the OEM channel above. Insurer co-funding works like fleet UBI/telematics programs elsewhere: an insurer subsidizes part of the kit cost against a premium discount priced off the ADAS telemetry stream, cutting effective retrofit CAC ASSUMPTION and giving DeepGrid a second paying customer for the same install. Brogen and Jiyu need a perception supplier and don't build one, no channel conflict.

chunks.section: Fast case vs. slow case. The plan as financially modeled (§8) is a fast case: certificatio
chunks.text: Fast case vs. slow case. The plan as financially modeled (§8) is a fast case: certification, tapeout and first OEM engagement all land inside 12–18 months. Comparable mandate- driven hardware markets have historically taken 3–5 years to move from mandate announcement to stable incumbent share EXTERNAL REFERENCE . In the slow case, FY27– FY29 revenue rests almost entirely on government/defence and insurer-co-funded retrofit (this section) while certification and OEM engagement continue in the background with no committed date, the fast case is upside, not the base the company should be funded against. The three phases are the spine of this plan, so they are set out as a matrix rather than described in prose. Read Figure 8 as the answer to four questions per phase: who we sell to, through whom, at what price, and what has to be true before the next phase opens.

chunks.section: Channel architecture, who actually reaches 4,000 kits a month
chunks.text: Channel architecture, who actually reaches 4,000 kits a month This plan previously had no distribution or installation mechanism, which is the most common way an Indian hardware business fails. We are not going to build a national direct sales force or a workshop network, so the channel is the strategy: CHANNEL WHY THEY CARRY US WHAT THEY TAKE WHAT WE MUST GIVE THEM OEM dealer and service networks they already have the bays, the technicians and the customer dealer margin ASSUMPTION a fitment-ready kit and training NBFCs and CV financiers they decide what gets fitted on a financed truck, and a safer truck is a better loan a fee or bundled EMI margin ASSUMPTION a residual-value and claims argument Insurers a claims-reduction argument is their product, not just ours premium share or co- funded pilots ASSUMPTION telemetry, and evidence that claims fall 3PLs and freight aggregators they aggregate small operators into a single contract volume pricing fleet-level dashboards and compliance reporting Tyre / lubricant / service chains national footprint of bays already visited by every truck installation fee a kit installable in hours by a trained technician Direct only for large organised fleets, PSU/defence and yard operators, a pilot and an SLA The installation and service question, stated as an open cost. Every kit needs fitting, calibration and support for years. We do not own a single workshop bay, and at 4,000 kits a month we would need hundreds. Whoever owns the bay owns the customer relationship, so channel selection is also a decision about how much of the customer we keep. This plan’s position: accept partner-owned installation to reach scale, but keep the data rights contractually (§6 above) so the model improves even where the relationship is shared.

chunks.section: A second SKU for the fragmented base
chunks.text: A second SKU for the fragmented base The organised segment in §3 does not get us to 49,000 kits a year on its own, and the fragmented base will not pay ₹2.3L. The honest options are three, and this plan commits to the third: OPTION VERDICT Sell the ₹2.3L kit to everyone Rejected. The price does not survive contact with a sub-five-truck operator Ignore the fragmented base entirely Viable, but caps us at the organised segment and makes the FY32 number depend almost entirely on OEM line- fit A stripped compliance SKU, fewer sensors, our compute, priced against the box a small operator already knows, sold only through the channels above Adopted as a design target PLAN . Price point to be set from channel feedback, not from our cost-plus ASSUMPTION Beyond the kit: the owned-fleet rental option Every channel above sells the box or licenses the brain, DeepGrid never touches the truck's ownership. That is one of three business models global autonomous trucking has already proven out, and the other two both involve owning or operating the vehicle: EXTERNAL REFERENCE Aurora Innovation licenses the "Aurora Driver" compute-and-software stack to OEMs and carriers per mile, asset-light, closest to DeepGrid's current model; Gatik owns or leases and directly operates a fleet of box trucks running fixed, repeatable middle- mile retail routes, asset-heavy, selling delivery capacity, not a component; Kodiak Robotics blends highway driver-out technology licensing with government/off-road contracts and some owned-fleet operation, a hybrid. These are widely reported industry structures, not figures from DeepGrid's own materials, and are not independently verified in this pass.

chunks.section: The uncomfortable reading, kept in deliberately. Against imports we are three times
chunks.text: The uncomfortable reading, kept in deliberately. Against imports we are three times cheaper. Against the device that actually wins mandated volume in India we are twenty times more expensive. Both statements are true, and a serious investor will find the second one. Our answer has to be that we are not selling into the same job: a ₹5,000 box satisfies an inspector, while our kit is what an OEM can put on a production line and a fleet can build a safety case on. That answer only holds if (a) enforcement eventually becomes real, (b) we win OEM line-fit, and (c) we field a stripped SKU for the segment that only wants compliance (§6). If none of those three lands, the low end takes the mandate and we are left with the organised segment alone. Moat, in order of durability: Structural price floor: owned silicon at <$3–4/bare die (₹1,750 packaged, §5) makes the ₹2.3L price ours to hold; importers cannot follow down without destroying their own margin stack. Certification + sovereignty: claimed only-indigenous AIS-validated chipset, AIS-004 native, 15 patents filed; foreign silicon excluded from government/defence fleets (§2). Certification is a path, not held, the killer risk, §10. Data moat that compounds, narrower than it sounds. D-Drive trained on Indian roads (cattle, autos, unmarked lanes, fog, no HD maps); the retrofit flywheel, sell the mirror, own the miles, upgrade in place, widens the gap with every kit (contractual per §6).

The photon-to-brake artifact (§6): one certifiable end-to-end latency number no bolt- together integration can reproduce. The real clock on this moat ASSUMPTION : because Bosch and Continental already have India manufacturing and AIS relationships, the window in which DeepGrid is the only India- priced, India-trained option is open only until one of them decides this niche is worth a product line, plausibly a matter of quarters, not the 12–24 months this plan's timeline implicitly assumes. chunks.text: Three things this changes. chunks.section: WHY A SECOND TRANCHE LATER FAILS
chunks.text: WHY A SECOND TRANCHE LATER FAILS CONSEQUENCE Clawback against a non-resident is messy. Share buyback or transfer at a pre-agreed price runs into FEMA transfer-pricing constraints The clawback we were relying on as the enforcement lever is the weakest part of the old structure, not the strongest What replaces the tranche gate. The instrument is CCPS with a milestone-linked conversion ratio. The investor funds $1M now and is fully invested; how many equity shares the CCPS converts into flexes with the agreed growth milestones. CCPS expressly support performance-linked milestones and valuation-linked conversion ratios SOURCED , and because the money is received at a single certified price, the FEMA problem above never arises. Economically it delivers what the clawback was meant to deliver, fewer shares on conversion is the same thing as a higher effective entry price, but it is executable, which the clawback may not be. Two things we accept in exchange, and should say plainly rather than discover later: the company gives up the discipline of withheld cash, and a conversion-ratio adjustment is contested at conversion rather than settled by simply not wiring money ASSUMPTION . In return we get the capital in full at the only price at which this entry is lawfully and defensibly available, now, and the certification and tapeout programme is funded without a gap in the middle of it.

# RISK CLASS WHY IT BITES MITIGATION 9 Asset-heavy expansion, if pursued low DeepGrid Fleet converts a semiconductor margin profile into a utilization-sensitive fleet-operator one. Ring-fenced post-Series-A SPV with an NBFC partner; never funded from this raise; pre- committed utilization (§6). 11 Fragmented base and no channel high About 75–80% of Indian operators own fewer than five trucks and ~3.5M operators move most of the freight SOURCED . The FY32 plan needs ~4,000 kits a month, and we own no installation or service network. Channel architecture in §6, OEM dealers, NBFCs, insurers, 3PLs, service chains; addressable segment narrowed in §3; installer- training and spares cost added to the Series-A model. 12 ASP erosion and the low- end competitor high AIS-140 devices sell at ₹4,500–11,000 today into an extremely price-sensitive base, with value migrating to platform SaaS SOURCED . Our ₹2.3L is ~20× that anchor, and transitional enforcement rewards cheap compliance. Compete on the OEM line-fit job rather than the inspector job (§7); field a stripped compliance SKU through channel (§6); attach the recurring software line early; carry an ASP-erosion case in the Series- A model (§8). 10 · NEW, incumbent fast-follow and enforcement-capacity risk. Continental and Bosch already manufacture in India with existing AIS relationships (§7); the window in which DeepGrid is the only India-priced, India-trained option closes the moment either decides this niche is worth a product line, plausibly within a few quarters, not the 12–24 months this plan's timeline assumes ASSUMPTION .

Separately, "enforcement is transitional" (§2) is itself an assumption: Indian vehicle-safety mandate enforcement has historically tracked inspection-infrastructure capacity (ARAI/ICAT testing-agency throughput) as much as policy intent, and neither this plan nor its sources model that capacity directly NOT IN GROUNDING . Mitigation: treat OEM design-in as upside, not a dated milestone (§6); fund FY27–FY29 primarily from government/defence and insurer-co- funded retrofit, which do not depend on either clock; revisit competitive intelligence on Bosch/Continental's India ADAS roadmap each quarter as a standing board item. 11 KPIs and what we will not do The operating dashboard. Every line is either already instrumented or must be before the metric is quoted externally:

KPI TARGET CADENCE Kits shipped per plan (§8) monthly Kit gross margin by phase 45% → ~72% monthly Certification milestone vs plan months 12–18 monthly, the #1 board metric OEM evaluations entered 1 within 12 months quarterly Retrofit fleet deals signed 1 within 9 months monthly Per-vehicle CAC / payback / LTV-CAC set at first fleet deal quarterly Day-30 field uptime set at first pilot monthly, the renewal driver (§5) Data-rights coverage of installed base 100% of new contracts quarterly Software ARPU vs commodity floor above ₹3–5k/yr quarterly Phase-3 supervision ratio better than 1:2 per site, monthly Phase-3 incidents zero per site, continuous Cash runway vs tapeout date ≥6 months buffer monthly Incumbent intel (Bosch / Continental India) standing item quarterly (§10 risk 10) Kits installed per active channel partner set at first channel deal monthly, the distribution metric (§6) Trained installers certified to be set monthly Realised ASP vs ₹2.3L plan ≥90% of plan quarterly, the erosion tripwire (§8) What we will NOT do before Series A, the focus covenant: no public-road driverless; no merchant silicon sales; no non-trucking verticals. A 5-person team funds exactly one tapeout and one vehicle program. We do not own or operate vehicle fleets from this raise, do not take vehicle-level integration as a business line, and do not book Phase-3 or DeepGrid Fleet (§6) revenue before, respectively, the private-land legal opinion exists or a dedicated fleet- financing SPV is closed, both stay explicitly outside this plan's capital until each is separately funded.

chunks.section: You have offered to come in as an investor, and separately you have said you would
chunks.text: Shravan, You have offered to come in as an investor, and separately you have said you would like to come in as a co-founder and bring your experience taking businesses international. I want to take the second offer more seriously than the first, because I think it is worth more to this company than the cheque, and because it deserves a real answer rather than an enthusiastic one. So I have written you a document about America specifically, kept apart from our India plan. I did that deliberately. Our India story is genuinely strong, and if I had merged the two you would have found the Indian tailwind quietly carrying the American argument. You would have discovered that yourself in month four, and you would have been right to be annoyed about it. What follows is what I actually believe, including the parts that make our US position look smaller than a founder normally admits in writing. Where a number is from our own material I have said so; where it is from outside research I have cited it. Everything I have not verified is marked as an assumption. I would rather you enter this knowing exactly what is unproven than have you find out after you have put your name on it. There is one thing I want to say plainly at the start. I take delivery, the silicon, the certification, the engineering. I am proposing that you take the market, starting with America. That is not me handing you the hard part while I keep the interesting one. In this company, market access is the scarcer of the two. 1 What I’m proposing, in one page Before the analysis, the proposal itself, so you can read everything after this knowing where it lands: WHAT MY PROPOSAL Your role Co-founder, international. You own US and global go-to-market: positioning, channel, partnerships, pricing proposals.

chunks.section: You have offered to come in as an investor, and separately you have said you would
chunks.text: I own delivery: silicon, RTL, certification, tapeout.

WHAT MY PROPOSAL Your investment Unchanged from what we discussed, $1M at ₹112 Cr pre-money, in two tranches, with the side letter. Your US upside Founder equity in the American company, earned in tranches against named commercial gates, with the first tranche vesting at signing. The Indian parent holds majority and the IP; you hold real founder shares in the entity you build. Full structure, guardrails and the dilution question in §8. What I am NOT asking you to fund America. The ₹45 Cr round funds India: the tapeout and AIS certification. No US spend draws on it. What I am asking you for Three conversations I cannot get on my own, and the judgement to tell me when I am wrong about this market. Details in §10. What this document does not do Forecast US revenue. There is no US line in our financial plan and I am not going to invent one before you and I have had a real partner conversation. The one-sentence version. I think America is a real opportunity for us, I think it is a licensing and stack business rather than the box business we run in India, and I think it is worth roughly nothing without someone who can open doors I cannot, which is the entire reason I am writing to you rather than putting a US slide in the India deck. 2 Why I did not simply extend the India plan Our India thesis rests on three things: a compliance mandate that creates demand by law, a price advantage of roughly three times against imported kits, and a sovereignty rule that excludes foreign silicon from government fleets. It is a good thesis. I have stress-tested it hard, and I believe it. None of those three exists in the United States.

I went through it line by line, and each row below kills a specific argument I might otherwise have been tempted to carry across: WHAT WE RELY ON IN INDIA INDIA UNITED STATES DOES IT TRAVEL? Demand driver GSR 184(E) compliance mandate Insurance and litigation economics SOURCED No

chunks.section: WHAT WE RELY ON IN INDIA
chunks.text: WHAT WE RELY ON IN INDIA INDIA UNITED STATES DOES IT TRAVEL? Regulatory instrument live since April 2026 AEB rule still only a supplemental proposed rule, and factory-fit at that SOURCED No Price umbrella ₹6.5–15L imports vs our ₹2.3L incumbents already at $27–60 per vehicle per month SOURCED No Sovereignty advantage Atmanirbhar excludes foreign silicon no equivalent, though China/ Russia restrictions help a non-China supplier SOURCED Inverted Smart mirror as a mirror replacement a permitted product FMVSS 111 still requires mirrors; camera systems only under research SOURCED No An open retrofit channel fragmented, no incumbent owned by Samsara, Lytx, Motive, Netradyne, SmartWitness SOURCED No Private-land driverless our Phase-3 margin engine same logic, and commercially proven by Outrider SOURCED Yes Cost-down silicon the whole moat still real, but sold to a platform, not to a fleet Partly What that table forced me to accept. In India we sell a finished kit to a fleet against a deadline. In America the product, the buyer and the trigger all fail at once. The only honest posture left is to sell the layer nobody else localises, our silicon, our IP and our model, into companies that already own the American fleet relationship, plus yard autonomy where no federal vehicle standard applies at all. That is a smaller and less glamorous claim than our India plan makes. I would rather hand you a smaller claim that survives contact. 3 What the American market actually looks like The opportunity is large and the buying trigger is money rather than law. American fleets do not buy safety hardware because a regulator compels them; they buy it because a single verdict can exceed the equity value of the business.

chunks.section: WHAT WE RELY ON IN INDIA
chunks.text: You will know this world better than I do, these are the numbers I have been working from:

US MARKET FACT VALUE AS OF EVIDENCE Class 8 trucks in operation (the retrofit base) 3.91M 2026 SOURCED New Class 8 retail sales, forecast 224,800 units 2026, +5.7% YoY SOURCED North American Class 8 production, forecast 274,111 units 2026, +9% YoY SOURCED US trucking industry revenue $906B 2024, 76.9% of freight SOURCED Driver shortage 60,000– 80,000 now; ~160,000 by 2031 (ATA) SOURCED Median trucking nuclear verdict $51M 2024 SOURCED Growth in $10M+ verdicts +235% 2009–2023 SOURCED Commercial auto liability cost growth 10.1%/yr since 2016 SOURCED Insurer discount for safety tech + training 15–20% 2026, major carriers SOURCED Yard / shuttle autonomy market $64B global 52.7% CAGR to 2030 (ABI Research) SOURCED The three rulemakings that decide our timing I want you to have these dates precisely, because they are the difference between a US plan and a US hope: RULEMAKING WHERE IT STANDS, AUGUST 2026 WHAT IT MEANS FOR US Heavy-vehicle AEB (NHTSA / FMCSA) Supplemental proposed rule expected July 2026; pending about three years; NHTSA’s false- activation engineering analysis open since Oct 2025 SOURCED A future factory-fit requirement on new Class 7–8, proposed 2027 and medium- duty 2028. That is an OEM and Tier-1 opportunity, not a retrofit market. FMVSS 111 / camera monitor systems NHTSA still researching, responding to petitions including one from Daimler Trucks North America; no final rule SOURCED Our smart mirror cannot be sold as a mirror replacement in America. It becomes a supplementary sensor pod alongside retained mirrors, which is a different product and a different pitch.

RULEMAKING WHERE IT STANDS, AUGUST 2026 WHAT IT MEANS FOR US California heavy-duty AV rules Finalised 28 April 2026. Vehicles over 10,001 lb permitted through staged permits; 500,000 test miles per phase; safety case filed with the DMV SOURCED The largest freight state is open. The mileage bar also tells us plainly that long- haul autonomy is not a business for a company our size. Commerce connected- vehicle rule Software prohibitions live 17 March 2026 for China/Russia nexus; hardware from MY2030 or 1 Jan 2029; passenger vehicles first, a truck rule signalled SOURCED This one is in our favour. India is not a restricted country, so we are a compliant non-China alternative at exactly the moment American OEMs are being pushed to find one. Why now, and why the window is real. Insurance economics are already forcing safety hardware onto American trucks faster than any regulator is. The AEB rule will convert that into factory-fit demand around 2027–2028. And the connected-vehicle rule is actively pushing OEMs to find non-Chinese silicon in that same window. That intersection is our entry, and it is open for roughly as long as our India certification window is, which is why I would rather start the American conversations now, cheaply, than later at scale. 4 Where I think we can win, and what I will not pretend Three routes survive §2. Two more I am naming and rejecting, because a plan that does not say what it refuses is not a plan: # ROUTE WHO BUYS WHY IT SURVIVES IN TIME V2 Yard and private- land autonomy ports, intermodal, plants, 3PL yards No FMVSS applies, no AV permit, no supply- longevity commitment.

Outrider has already proven customers buy this as a subscription in a $64B market SOURCED First V3 Supplementary sensor pod fleets, through a platform partner Blind-spot and side detection without touching FMVSS 111; rides a partner’s existing install base Second V1 Silicon, IP and module supply platform vendors, Tier-1s, truck OEMs They own the fleet relationship and the certification burden; we own a cost floor they cannot match, and the connected-vehicle rule makes a non-China supplier structurally attractive SOURCED Last, see below

# ROUTE WHO BUYS WHY IT SURVIVES IN TIME X1 Long-haul driverless autonomy, I am rejecting this. Aurora, Kodiak and Waabi are years and hundreds of millions ahead (§6), and California alone wants 500,000 test miles per phase never, in this plan X2 Direct fleet retrofit sales, I am rejecting this too. Samsara, Lytx, Motive and Netradyne own that channel at $27–60 per vehicle per month with software bundled in SOURCED never, in this plan The gate on V1 that I only learned by asking properly This is the most useful thing in the document, and it is not flattering to us. American automotive buyers now expect guaranteed part availability measured in decades, STMicroelectronics extended its automotive MCU longevity programme to 20 years, guaranteeing supply to at least 2038 SOURCED , and Tier-1 supply increasingly involves multi-year volume or take-or-pay commitments SOURCED . Functional safety at ASIL-D additionally requires single-point-fault coverage above 99% under a managed process with independent assessment SOURCED, a programme, not a certificate you buy late. Read plainly: a five-person fabless company with one shuttle tapeout cannot sign a fifteen-year longevity commitment or a credible second-source plan. Not price, not performance, not our AI, that is what would end a Tier-1 conversation about selling them a chip today. V1 becomes real when a foundry or a Tier-1 stands behind the supply promise, or when we license the IP instead of selling the part. Which turns out to be the strategically interesting answer, and it leads directly into the next section. 5 What we would actually sell them When I say “component supplier,” I do not mean our India kit taken apart and sold as pieces.

Our kit’s value is integration, and breaking an assembly into parts is a worse business than selling the assembly. What travels to America is narrower and deeper: the layers where we own the intellectual property. It is also worth being explicit about what we do not make, because those are exactly the things people assume a “full-stack” company sells:

NOT OURS TO SELL WHOSE IT IS WHY I WILL NOT SELL IT Drive-by-wire / brake-by-wire Jiyu Technology, our partner ASIL-D chassis-by-wire with redundant braking, already shipping to 30+ OEMs. We integrate against it and certify a latency budget into it. Reselling it earns us no margin and builds us no moat. Steer-by-wire Jiyu and incumbent Tier-1s Same reasoning. Actuation is a partner domain by design. Chassis, e-axles, trailers Brogen EV, our partner A commodity by 2026, and not a semiconductor business. Cameras and image sensors sensor and module vendors Bought-in parts inside our pod. We do not fabricate image sensors and I will not let a deck imply we do. 77 GHz radar module radar Tier-1s Our radar work is a front-end chip needing SiGe BiCMOS, not a finished module PLAN . An FPGA cannot prototype a 77 GHz front end, so it is proven on silicon or not at all. That makes it a 2028+ item, not a US entry product. LiDAR, Not in our stack. Our perception thesis is camera plus radar, no HD maps. What we do own falls into six sellable things. The column I would draw your attention to is the fourth one:

chunks.text: Why that fourth column changes the plan. S1, S2 and S6 carry no longevity gate and no automotive silicon qualification at all, nobody demands a fifteen-year supply commitment on a soft-IP licence, a software model, or a private-land stack. S4, the packaged chip, is the biggest prize and the one thing we genuinely cannot sell into automotive yet. So the ladder is S2 and S6 first, S1 and S3 next, S4 last, and the honest conclusion is that our first American revenue is far more likely to be a licence than a part. I want to flag what that implies about the job, because it affects whether this partnership is the right fit rather than just an attractive one. Selling soft IP or a perception model to a Tier-1 is a long-cycle, technical, relationship-led enterprise sale, much closer to licensing than to distribution. If that is the kind of selling you have done, this works. If your strength is channel and volume distribution, then S6, yard autonomy, is where you should start, and we should both know that going in. 6 What it costs to play in this category I would rather show you this than have you discover it. chunks.section: 7 The competitive set, and the posture I propose
chunks.text: 7 The competitive set, and the posture I propose for each There are two distinct competitive groups in America, and I think our correct relationship differs for each. Confusing them produces a plan that competes with everyone and partners with no one: COMPANY WHAT THEY ARE WHERE THEY STAND IN 2026 MY PROPOSED POSTURE Aurora Long-haul driverless; licenses the Driver 5.3M cumulative miles to April 2026; about 440,000 driverless miles by end June; 10 Sun Belt routes; second- generation trucks July 2026; Roush targeting 1,000 trucks a year; one customer ordering 500 SOURCED Do not compete Kodiak (Kodiak AI) Driverless technology plus owned operations Public via Ares Acquisition Corp II, Sept 2025; 30 power units; driverless frac-sand for Atlas Energy; long-haul driverless targeted 2H 2026; partnered with Bosch to scale hardware SOURCED Do not compete, but their Bosch deal is the exact template for our V1 Waabi Autonomous trucking, simulation-first Raised $1B; investors include NVIDIA’s NVentures, Volvo Group VC, Porsche SE SOURCED Do not compete Gatik Owns and operates a middle-mile fleet Asset-heavy operator Not our lane Outrider Yard autonomy as a subscription $62M raised; driverless rollout 2026; taking 2026–27 orders; enterprise support launched SOURCED Proof that V2 works, compete or supply Samsara, Lytx, Motive, Netradyne, SmartWitness Fleet safety platforms, they own the retrofit channel The five vendors dominating the 2026 US fleet camera market SOURCED Partner. Do not fight. V1 and V3 both route through them If you take one datapoint from this table, take the Kodiak–Bosch arrangement. An American autonomy company chose to partner with a component supplier to scale its hardware.

chunks.text: That is the seat I am asking you to help us apply for, and it exists partly because of the connected-vehicle rule, not only because of our cost. 8 The structure: investor in India, founder in America Let me state your proposal as I now understand it, because it is cleaner than the version I had been arguing with myself about: # WHAT YOU PROPOSED MY ANSWER 1 You invest in the Indian company today, $1M for ~7.7% at ₹112 Cr pre-money Agreed. Terms as already discussed, side letter included 2 You come in as a founder in the American company Agreed, with the guardrails below 3 Your American equity is earned against performance as we go, not granted at signing Agreed, and it was going to be my proposal too 4 We then raise a $25M follow-on in the US to compete properly Agreed, this is §10, with one caveat about the word “compete” So we are aligned on the shape. What I want to write down are the four things that have to be true for this structure to survive diligence in 2028 rather than need surgery. Three of them protect you as much as me; one of them is mine and I am not going to move on it. The structure at inception A Delaware entity, majority-owned by Deepgrid Semi, with you as founder holding earned equity. Illustratively, and these percentages are a starting point for negotiation, not a position ASSUMPTION : HOLDER AT INCEPTION NOTES Deepgrid Semi (Indian parent) majority Funded as an ODI. Holds the exclusive US licence; the IP itself stays in India You, as co-founder meaningful minority, earned in tranches Real founder equity, not phantom, vesting against the gates below

HOLDER AT INCEPTION NOTES US employee pool reserved For the American hires you will need Later: the $25M round dilutes everyone pro-rata Including me, including the parent The four guardrails # GUARDRAIL WHY IT PROTECTS YOU WHY IT PROTECTS THE COMPANY 1 The Indian parent holds majority and control of the US entity It is what makes your shares fundable. An institutional lead in 2028 needs one clear owner of the technology behind the entity it is buying into Our ₹204 Cr investors keep the upside of the market they backed us to reach 2 The IP stays with the Indian parent. The US entity holds an exclusive, territory- and field-of-use-limited licence You are selling something with a real owner standing behind it, not a shell with borrowed rights One asset, one owner. This is the guardrail I will not move on, every other term is negotiable 3 Your equity is earned in tranches against named commercial gates, with standard leaver and reverse- vesting provisions You will be able to point at delivered outcomes rather than explain a founder title to every future investor It makes a generous grant defensible on the cap table instead of looking like a gift 4 ODI filed properly, and your FEMA residency established before we paper anything It is your shares that are at risk if the structure is later found non- compliant A FEMA contravention discovered during 2028 diligence is a repriced or dead round What “earned” would actually mean I would rather agree the tranches now, in writing, than have a conversation in month nine about whether something counted. My proposal is that your equity vests in four roughly equal parts against the gates already in §9 and §10:

TRANCHE VESTS ON ROUGHLY WHEN T-A Signing, you join, the entity is formed, US0 begins on execution T-B US1, one signed technical evaluation with a platform vendor or Tier-1 months 3–9 T-C US3, one live US yard reference, or a first smaller-OEM evaluation months 9–18 T-D The $25M round closes, the outcome that makes all of this real 2028 Note what tranche A does: you hold founder equity from day one, not after a probation. The gates govern the rest. I think that is the right balance between your point that you are a founder rather than an employee, and my point that a title should be earned where the work is invisible. The dilution question, since it is the one you should press me on Your percentage will fall when we raise $25M. Mine falls too, and so does the parent’s. The honest framing is that your return comes from the entity being worth something, not from the percentage being large, a meaningful minority of a company that raised $25M on real American traction is worth many multiples of a large slice of a 2026 shell that no investor will price. That is the whole argument, and it is also why I keep insisting on one clean cap table: the 2028 round is exactly what a fragmented structure would make expensive or impossible. Two protections I would offer against that dilution without hesitation: pro-rata rights so you can defend your position in the round, and a written commitment that your unvested tranches are adjusted rather than crushed if the round is larger or earlier than planned ASSUMPTION .

What Indian law constrains Not a free design space, and I would rather we both know this before counsel tells us: CONSTRAINT WHAT IT MEANS HERE FEMA / ODI: where an Indian resident has control of a foreign entity it constitutes overseas direct investment, reportable through the AD bank on Form ODI Part I / Form FC, even where no cash is remitted SOURCED The parent’s majority holding in the US entity is a reportable ODI. We structure and file it properly at inception, not retrospectively.

CONSTRAINT WHAT IT MEANS HERE Resident-individual restriction: a FEMA-resident individual generally cannot acquire control in a foreign entity that itself has an Indian subsidiary or step-down subsidiary SOURCED Your FEMA residency status determines what you can hold, and we need it established first. It is also a reason the US entity should sit under the Indian parent rather than above it ASSUMPTION . Flip timing: the gradual-migration route is what is normally recommended early, because it avoids ODI share-swap complexity and does not crystallise capital gains SOURCED If the 2028 lead wants a Delaware topco, that route stays open, provided we have kept one clean cap table until then. The one caveat on the word “compete.” $25M does not compete with the companies in §7, they have raised about $5.6B between them. What $25M does is fund qualification, a US presence, longevity backing and working capital so that we can win the segments we chose in §4 and §10: smaller and vocational OEMs, terminal tractors and yards, module and licence supply. That is a fight we can win. Head-on long-haul autonomy is not, at any round size we will realistically raise, and I would rather we say that to a US investor before they say it to us. Where I have landed. Yes to investor in India today. Yes to founder in America. Yes to earned equity, generously sized, with tranche A vesting at signing. Yes to the $25M follow- on. The two things I am asking you to accept in exchange are that the Indian parent keeps majority and control of the US entity, and the IP stays with the parent under an exclusive licence. If you can live with those two, I think we have a deal and the rest is counsel and percentages.
9 How I would sequence it, and the risks I’d rather you hear from me Sequenced so nothing expensive happens before something cheap has been proven. No stage below draws on the ₹45 Cr round:

STAGE MONTHS FROM SIGNING WHAT WE WOULD HAVE WHAT IT COSTS US0, Access 0–3 A target list of platform vendors and Tier-1s, warm introductions, one non- binding technical conversation travel only US1, Validation 3–9 One signed technical evaluation with a platform or Tier-1, this is also your side-letter enterprise/ISV milestone engineering time US2, Qualification scoping 6–12 A written quote and timeline for AEC- Q100 / IATF 16949 / ISO 26262, the real cost of playing, priced instead of guessed study cost only US3, Yard reference 9–18 One US private-land yard pilot, where no FMVSS or AV permit applies partner-funded or a separate SPV US4, Entity and first agreement 18+ US entity, Declaration-of-Conformity readiness, first supply or licence agreement gated on Series A, not this round And the risks. I have put the two I find most uncomfortable at the top: # RISK CLASS WHY IT BITES WHAT I PROPOSE WE DO U7 US product liability high I have been quoting that $51M median verdict as a sales argument. It is also our exposure: a perception component sits inside the liability chain of an 80,000 lb vehicle in the most litigious trucking market in the world ASSUMPTION . The tail risk exceeds this entire round. US counsel before any US revenue; product-liability cover as a priced cost line, not an afterthought; limitation-of- liability and indemnity caps in every agreement; our bit-exact deterministic replay as the forensic defence. U1 Automotive qualification is unfunded high AEC-Q100, IATF 16949 and ISO 26262 all precede any Tier-1 design-in, and none is funded in the ₹45 Cr ASSUMPTION . US2 exists purely to price this before we commit. V2 needs none of it and can produce our first US reference without it.

U2 No US entity, team or track record high A five-person Hyderabad company has no US legal presence, no automotive references, no local support. This is the whole reason the lane needs you rather than a hire. US4 gates entity spend to Series A. U3 Channel dependence high V1 and V3 both run through partners who can drop us, second- source us, or build it themselves. Run V1 and V2 in parallel so no single partner is load-bearing. Our cost floor is the reason to keep us.

# RISK CLASS WHY IT BITES WHAT I PROPOSE WE DO U8 FEMA / ODI structuring medium Control of a foreign entity from India is reportable ODI even with no cash moved SOURCED . Structure per option A in §8; file properly; keep a later flip available. U4 The truck connected- vehicle rule lands badly medium Commerce has signalled a separate rule for trucks and buses; a broad foreign-nexus reading could sweep in non-China suppliers too SOURCED . Counsel before US4. Declaration-of- Conformity readiness as a named deliverable. U5 The AEB rule slips again medium Already about three years pending with an open false-activation analysis SOURCED . Insurance-driven demand does not depend on the rule. V2 depends on neither. U6 India execution suffers high My attention and scarce engineering time pulled toward a market with no near-term revenue. A hard rule I am imposing on myself: no India engineer is assigned to US work before AIS certification closes. The honest bottom line. There is a real market here, a real buying trigger, and a real structural opening for a non-Chinese silicon and IP supplier. There is also no US revenue I am willing to forecast, no qualification budget in this round, and no American presence today. What I am proposing is that we buy an option on America with your network rather than with the company’s capital, and that you and I judge it on whether US1 and US2 close on time, not on the size of the American market. 10 The 2028 round, and the asset that unlocks it You made a point in conversation that I think is the strongest strategic idea either of us has put on the table, and it deserves to be in this document rather than left in a phone call.

Your argument, as I understood it: once Indian trucks are actually running with our ADAS, that fleet becomes the reference that opens America, and it is the smaller US OEMs, not the majors, who will want to try it. Their interest is what makes a US round raisable, and we should raise roughly $25M in America in 2028 to convert that interest into a business.

chunks.section: I agree with it, I think it is better than anything I had written, and it fixes the one re
chunks.text: I agree with it, I think it is better than anything I had written, and it fixes the one real hole in this document: everything up to §9 ends at “gated on Series A” with no American capital plan at all. So here is that plan, with the parts I would push back on marked as such. Why the reference asset changes our position Today I walk into an American conversation with measured silicon and a good story. In 2028, if India goes the way BP-1A says it should, I walk in with something categorically different, a deployed fleet, field-failure data from a punishing duty cycle, and manufacturing maturity somebody else has already paid to prove. No amount of pitching substitutes for that, and it is the one asset the companies in §7 cannot simply buy with funding. But I want to be precise about what it proves, because overselling this is how the document would lose its credibility: THE INDIA FLEET PROVES IT DOES NOT PROVE Reliability at a hostile duty cycle, heat, vibration, dust, voltage transients, tamper resistance over real months US regulatory compliance. AIS certification is not FMVSS, and the test protocols differ Manufacturing and field maturity, that we can build, install, support and service at volume US highway perception validation. Indian road data does not validate American interstate conditions Unit economics at real volume, our cost floor demonstrated rather than modelled Automotive qualification. AEC-Q100 / IATF 16949 / ISO 26262 still have to be done and paid for (§9, U1) That the model works on messy roads, arguably harder than US highways Anything about longevity. A deployed fleet is not a 15-year supply guarantee (§4) Why smaller OEMs, and which ones Your instinct to skip the majors is the part I most agree with.

chunks.section: I agree with it, I think it is better than anything I had written, and it fixes the one re
chunks.text: Daimler, Paccar and Volvo have entrenched Tier-1 relationships, multi-year qualification programmes and no particular reason to take our call in 2028. The smaller and vocational American OEMs are a genuinely different buyer: WHY THEY ARE REACHABLE EVIDENCE They face the same AEB requirement with no in- house ADAS capability and no Tier-1 leverage the rule targets new Class 7–8 from 2027 and medium-duty 2028 SOURCED ADAS is already arriving in vocational, so the segment will be actively shopping Mack has scheduled a comprehensive ADAS suite for a new vocational platform with late-2027 builds SOURCED

WHY THEY ARE REACHABLE EVIDENCE They are structurally underserved by incumbents because their volumes are small structural ASSUMPTION Several build terminal tractors and spotter trucks, the exact vehicle our yard stack runs on Autocar builds severe-duty vocational trucks and terminal tractors SOURCED ; Battle Motors builds refuse, infrastructure and a non-CDL Class 6 SOURCED The convergence I had missed until I looked at the target list properly. A maker like Autocar builds both severe-duty vocational trucks and terminal tractors SOURCED . That means the same OEM is simultaneously an ADAS customer and a yard-autonomy platform partner, our S3 module and our S6 stack sold to one buyer, on one relationship, through one integration. Every other route in §4 needs a different partner for each product. This one does not, which makes the smaller-OEM segment our best single target rather than merely the easiest one. Your point also forces a correction on my own SKU logic. In §5 I argued the licence SKUs come first because they dodge the longevity gate. That holds for Tier-1s and autonomy companies, who have their own engineering teams. Smaller OEMs are the opposite: they lack integration capacity, so they want a more complete product, not bare RTL. For this buyer the order is S3 (compute module), S5 (sensor pod) and S6 (yard stack), with S1 becoming what we license to the majors later. That is a real change to the plan, and it came from your framing rather than mine. The round itself On the number and the timing: I think 2028 is right, and I would treat $25M as the correct order of magnitude rather than a figure either of us should defend yet ASSUMPTION .

WHAT THE ROUND WOULD FUND WHY IT CANNOT BE FUNDED EARLIER Automotive qualification, AEC-Q100, IATF 16949, ISO 26262, PPAP The unfunded gate in §9 (U1), and the thing that converts us from a licensor into a supplier US entity, local field-applications and support presence No American OEM designs in a part with no local support, and premature before there is a design-in to support Inventory and working capital for module supply Only meaningful once an OEM has committed volume A longevity and second-source posture, foundry commitments behind a 15-year promise Needs capital and a foundry relationship we will not have before the 28 nm part is in production

chunks.section: Why 2028 rather than sooner or later: the AEB factory-fit requirement bites on new Class 7
chunks.text: Why 2028 rather than sooner or later: the AEB factory-fit requirement bites on new Class 7–8 from 2027 and medium-duty in 2028 SOURCED ; vocational ADAS platforms are being built for late 2027 SOURCED ; California’s heavy-duty framework opened in April 2026 SOURCED ; and our India reference will by then be mature rather than anecdotal. Those four line up exactly once. And this is where your equity question answers itself. A $25M US-led round in 2028 is precisely the trigger event I described in §8: the moment a Delaware topco becomes the right structure, and the round that prices your founder equity in the American company at a valuation set by an American lead investor rather than by me, and the final vesting tranche in §8. A meaningful minority of a company that raised $25M on real traction is worth many multiples of a large slice of a 2026 shell nobody will price. It is also why I care so much about not fragmenting the cap table now, a fragmented structure is exactly what would make the 2028 round expensive or impossible. What has to be true by then So that we are both measuring the same things.

Three things I cannot get on my own: # WHAT I AM ASKING WHY IT HAS TO BE YOU 1 One platform or Tier-1 technical conversation, Samsara, Motive, Netradyne class, or a truck Tier-1 I can build the part. I cannot get the first meeting, and a cold approach from an unknown Indian fabless company does not convert. 2 One American yard operator, a port, plant, intermodal or 3PL yard willing to run a pilot This is our fastest credible US reference and it needs no certification. It is also the deal I understand least well commercially. 3 Your judgement, used against me You have taken businesses international and I have not. If your read is that the licensing route is wrong, or the sequence is wrong, I want that in month one, not month ten. And what you get from me: the delivery half done properly and on record. First silicon, AIS certification, and a company where the numbers in front of an investor are labelled by how they were obtained. That is the part I can promise, and it is the part that makes your half sellable. What happens next STEP WHEN WHO You read this and BP-1A and tell me where you think I am wrong this week You We agree the pool size, the three gates, and the vesting schedule within two weeks Both Counsel drafts: subsidiary, incentive pool, side letter, conversion right weeks 2–4 Counsel, board- approved Signing, T1, and US0 begins week 4–5 Both First review of US0/US1 against the gates month 3 Both, with the board

chunks.section: D E E P G R I D S E M I · H Y D E R A B A D, R E A D E R ' S G U I D E
chunks.text: D E E P G R I D S E M I · H Y D E R A B A D, R E A D E R ' S G U I D E Six Pages, One Story, What to Look For on Each Each page carries the story to the next. If you have two minutes, read this page and look at the diagrams; if you have ten, read it front to back, it is written to be read in order. 1 · Introduction, one company, one chip, three industries Follow the diagram left to right: the chip with six chiplets drawn on the die, the ~$18M → ~$5M saving because it is one combo die, the three industries it feeds, one Sentience AI layer above all three, ending in Safer Roads, Indigenous Chips, Low Cost Chips. If you see only this page, you have understood the company. 2 · ADAS, the problem and the trigger Two things to see: the number 168,000 (road deaths every year), and the funnel, a government mandate turns those deaths into a ₹8,500 Cr compulsory market from April 2026, and our kit is 3–7× cheaper than any import because we own the chip inside it. 3 · DGrid Alpha, what the ₹50 Cr builds Three things: the platform diagram (one tapeout becomes four business lines, ₹1,388 Cr by FY32), the nested-circles market figure (we are the small green dot inside a $120 bn market, deliberately honest about our size), and the ask table, the chip itself is ₹18 Cr, one line item, not the whole round. 4 · Defence, proof, not promise The Army already pays us: ₹1.01 Cr contracted via MCEME. The scatter chart is the key picture, only one chip in the world does flight-control + navigation + AI together, imported at $1,200; we aim at the same corner at a fraction of the price. 5 · Industrial, one drawing of a warehouse GPS never works indoors.

chunks.section: D E E P G R I D S E M I · H Y D E R A B A D, P R E P A R E D F O R S H R A V A N & M A Y
chunks.text: D E E P G R I D S E M I · H Y D E R A B A D, P R E P A R E D F O R S H R A V A N & M A Y O O K H One Chip. Three Industries. Deepgrid Semi is an autonomous systems company from Hyderabad. We design a single indigenous chip, DGrid Alpha, and point it at three industries at once: vehicle safety on India's roads, defence robotics and drones, and the industrial silicon India imports today. One design investment, three revenue engines, zero import dependence. T H E V I S I O N, O N E C H I P, T H RE E I N D U S T RI E S , O N E I N T E LLI G E N C E A100 R100 T100 S100 D100 H100 DGrid Alpha one combo die · six chiplets built as separate chips: ~$18M in tapeouts as one combo die: ~$5M, the chiplet saving ADAS vehicle safety · India's trucks DEFENCE robots & drones · Army-proven INDUSTRIAL warehouse & indoor autonomy · UGV · AMR Sentience one AI intelligence layer across all three industries Safer Roads the mission Indigenous Chips designed in India Low Cost Chips priced for India One die, three industries, one intelligence. Six chiplets share a single combo die, built as separate chips they would cost ~$18M in tapeouts; as one die, ~$5M. The same silicon powers ADAS, Defence and Industrial products, and one Sentience AI layer learns across all three, delivering safer roads, indigenous chips, and low-cost chips. Cost figures are engineering estimates. T H E T H RE E I N D U S T RI E S, O N E S I LI C O N C O RE U N D E RN E AT H ADAS, Vehicle Safety India's roads are the world's deadliest, and the government has now made driver-assistance mandatory on commercial trucks, covering the national fleet. Imported kits are priced out of reach; ours is not, because we own the chip inside it.

chunks.text: Defence, Robots & Drones The Indian Army is already our paying customer, with hardware fielded and reviewed by senior command. The same die carries a military-grade chiplet, and India's first indigenous drone flight- control, navigation and AI chip. Industrial, Warehouse & Indoor Autonomy UGVs, AMRs and inventory drones for warehouses, factories and campuses, GPS never works indoors, and our autonomy stack was built for exactly that. A working load-carrying platform has already been demonstrated. How to read this document: the ADAS story follows next, then the investment in DGrid Alpha, then the Defence and Industrial pages, where we talk numbers. The final page is the long-horizon compute roadmap. That is the whole story in one picture. It begins where the pain is worst, on India's roads. → Deepgrid Semi Pvt Ltd · Strictly Confidential Introduction S T R I C T LY C O N F I D E N T I A L · F O R A U T H O R I S E D R E C I P I E N T S O N LY SHRAVAN & MAY OOKH

chunks.section: I N D U S T R Y 1 O F 3, A D A S · V E H I C L E S A F E T Y
chunks.text: I N D U S T R Y 1 O F 3, A D A S · V E H I C L E S A F E T Y India Loses 168,000 Lives on Its Roads Every Year. We Exist to End That. chunks.text: I N D U S T R Y 2 O F 3, D E F E N C E · R O B O T S & D R O N E S The Army Already Pays Us, And the Drone Chip Rides the Same Die Defence is not a promise on a slide: ₹1.01 Cr is contracted via MCEME / Indian Army, with hardware fielded and reviewed by senior command. The D100 chiplet turns the same DGrid Alpha tapeout into military-grade compute, lockstep RISC-V safety cores (ASIL-D path), AES-256 secure enclave, at zero additional design cost. W H Y F LI G H T C O N T RO L + V I O + A I M U S T LI V E O N O N E C H I P FC, Fly The flight-control loop keeps the drone in the air, real-time, deterministic, every millisecond. It cannot wait on another chip. VIO, Know Where You Are GPS is jammed along the LoC/LAC and never works indoors. Visual-inertial navigation is the only positioning that survives, geometry, not GPS. AI, See & Decide Onboard detection and obstacle avoidance when the comms link is gone, the drone must think for itself, on the drone. Fused on one die, they become a hardware fail-safe: when the link or GPS fails, the FC loop reads VIO position directly, same silicon, same clock, no bus, no second board, and flies itself home. Split across chips, that path gains latency, weight, power and failure points; a drone falling over a city or into stacked inventory is a lawsuit. No SoC vendor, Qualcomm, Ambarella, Hailo, sells a hardware-isolated fail-safe as a chip feature. Doing it in silicon is a defensible moat.

A six-chiplet 28 nm automotive SoC, taped out in gated stages, sold as fifteen products into a market where the demand date is written into law. ₹1,128 Cr of FY2032 revenue rests on one tapeout, which is the whole investment case, and the whole risk. The summary, if you read nothing else Deepgrid Semi is a one-chip company with fifteen ways to sell the same die. The chip is real, six RTL designs are tapeout-ready, a 130 nm tapeout is already done, and the perception stack runs at 40 fps on an FPGA today. The demand is real, India is writing ADAS into law for commercial vehicles, function by function, on dated deadlines. What is not yet reconciled is the schedule between them. Qualified silicon lands H1 2028 , after the last mandate date, and OEM design-in runs 18–30 months. So the next two years are an FPGA business sold through government and PSU channels, and that, not the ₹1,128 Cr terminal year, is what this round actually underwrites. Underwrite this, 01: Two products carry 64% of revenue. The truck kit and the smart mirror are one family sold to overlapping buyers. A certification delay hits ₹720 Cr at once. Underwrite this, 02: The FPGA window, not the ASIC. Nothing beyond FY2027’s ₹1.7 Cr happens without production silicon, and silicon arrives after every mandate date. Underwrite this, 03:

Three headline claims fail the company’s own controls. The mandate date, the ₹1 Cr defence revenue and the price comparison are all barred by its internal ledger, and printed anyway. The ask. Release capital against silicon, certification and paying customers. The $3.17M of tapeout NRE is already structured as four gates, and six of nine de-risking milestones are marked done before the round opens, so the forecast is the consequence of those gates, not the thing being funded. The argument in seven moves Demand is written into law Five ADAS functions become mandatory on commercial vehicles across 2027–28. Roughly a million N2/N3 units a year fall in scope. Foreign silicon prices India out An imported ADAS module costs multiples of the kit price this market can pay, and no indigenous alternative exists at this stage. So own the die Six chiplets on one 57 mm² part. Eleven sensor channels fused in 8.6 ms of a 33.3 ms frame. The headroom is the portfolio 74% of the frame is unused, so fifteen products across four surfaces run on one mask and one firmware stack. But the silicon arrives late Qualified parts land H1 2028, after every mandate date on the calendar, and design-in runs 18–30 months. This is the turn in the argument. So the FPGA window is the strategy Government and PSU units ship first, and the telemetry they generate is what makes the Tier-1 design-in winnable.
The round is priced against a ₹10.1 Cr trough That is the whole margin of safety, and two dated obligations land inside it, funded nowhere.

chunks.section: An autonomous systems company that builds its own silicon
chunks.text: Deepgrid Semi sells complete, certified autonomy systems. It builds the six-chiplet die underneath them because owning the chip is the only way to ship those systems at a price the Indian market can pay. Founded and led by Aravind Prasad G (20 years, multiple exits, Evolgence IT Solutions, Deepgrid Datacentre, Evolgence Energy), with Ayaz Khan as silicon architecture lead. Incorporated in Telangana (CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631), operating from T-Hub Phase 2, Knowledge City, Hyderabad. Thirty-four people today, 541 in the FY2032 plan. Angels are domain operators, including DFT and semiconductor engineers backing the company personally. The order of markets is deliberate: commercial fleets are the mandate wedge and are live now; OEM design-in is the platform prize; defence and robotics is optionality on the same silicon that is already earning revenue. About 88% of planned revenue is systems and products ; roughly 5% is merchant silicon. Why now

chunks.section: The demand is legislated, not forecast
chunks.text: India is putting ADAS into law for commercial vehicles function by function, each with its own standard and its own date. Read at the standards level, the version that survives diligence, the schedule is this: AEBS (AIS-162, CMVR 96(12)) binds new models 1 Jan 2027 and all models 1 Oct 2027; drowsiness, blind-spot, moving-off and lane-departure warning (AIS-184/186/187/188, CMVR 125Q and 98(6)) bind new models 1 Oct 2027 and all models 1 Jan 2028. The financial model sizes the reachable pool at ~500k new N2/N3 units a year plus a ~500k retrofit pool, 1.0M units . Four functions arriving on one clock is the commercial fact that matters. Every CV maker must source drowsiness, blind-spot, moving-off and lane-departure together, so a supplier that carries more than one of the four from a single perception core is materially easier to nominate than four separate suppliers. That, rather than any single function, is the design-in argument. Three further rules stack on top of the truck mandate. AIS-140 requires GPS and driver-behaviour monitoring on commercial fleets, the S100 chiplet carries that telematics interface natively, in every kit, at no added cost. AIS-004 puts LDWS, FCWS and LKAS on all new M-category vehicles, creating aftermarket retrofit pull for the ₹50,000 mirror. And post-2022 supply fragility has Indian OEMs actively seeking a domestic chip partner.

Five configurations of the same silicon, from passive alerts to full driverless, and one upgrade path that keeps the hardware already sold. Recurring revenue sits on top of every rung: SaaS at ₹5K–₹25K per vehicle per year, Autonomous Truck DaaS at ₹2.5L/truck/yr (93% GM) , seaport AGV fleet ops at ₹45.3L/AGV/yr (92% GM) , and fleet-health SaaS through the H100 wearable at ₹8L/truck/yr. The plan has recurring revenue reaching ₹116 Cr by FY2032. The portfolio

chunks.section: Six buyer routes off one bill of materials
chunks.text: The fifteen revenue lines reach market through genuinely different procurement motions, which is what keeps the concentration risk from being total.
Six cameras, two radars, LiDAR and drive-by-wire on an N2/N3 truck, certified to AIS-162/188. Fleet ROI under two years on insurance premium reduction alone.

Replacement mirror with display, four body cameras, a loom and a 15-minute fitment. No mandate applies, it sells as an accessory through fitment shops today, and builds the channel the harder products inherit.

Forklifts and tugs a site already owns, retrofitted to drive themselves. Geofenced, ≤25 km/h, ±5 cm obstacle stop. No homologation inside a private site, so L4 ships years before it is legal on a road.
The autonomous vehicle layer of container-terminal automation, sold as fleet operations rather than hardware. Electric, no fuel, 92% gross margin on the ops contract.
Humanoid, UGV and drone compute on the D100 secure enclave, AES-256, lockstep RISC-V, ECC SRAM. A sovereign procurement route that does not depend on the automotive mandate at all.

The core itself, licensed to an OEM rather than sold as a part. Starts FY2029 because a licence needs a track record, the only line in the plan with no BOM whatsoever. chunks.section: Six chiplets, one 57 mm² die, six independent revenue lines
chunks.text: This is the asset the round buys. Each chiplet is a separate business, and replicating the set would take six tapeouts. 32,768 MACs at 600 MHz gives a derived 39.3 TOPS INT8, architecture arithmetic, not a silicon measurement, with 102.4 GB/s of LPDDR5 bandwidth. The headroom is the product strategy: a drone stack, a wearable, a port AGV and a licensable core all fit inside the frame the truck kit leaves empty. PrimeSoC returned FEASIBLE on the architecture in March 2026. Two claims underneath that are worth separating from the TOPS number, because they are the ones competitors cannot patch around. Batch-dispatch firmware (Patent 1) decouples inference from RISC-V host supervision, keeping the ALU active far longer per cycle, the company’s answer to why headline TOPS on competing parts does not translate into delivered frames. And the R100’s 12-bit native radar ADC preserves dynamic range that every competitor re-quantises to INT16, which is what buys detection sensitivity in monsoon and fog. What it sees

chunks.section: Two retrofit mirror towers, and no blind spot left on the vehicle
chunks.text: The physical product is a pair of replacement mirror towers plus in-cab cameras and front/rear 77 GHz radar. It installs in 15–35 minutes, needs no separate sensor sourcing, and the same mirror is reused at every rung of the upgrade ladder, which is where the customer-retention argument comes from: switching away means losing the India-trained model. chunks.text: Revenue Institutional defence revenue earned on FPGA hardware before ASIC exists. The memorandum states ₹1 Cr; the company’s own claim controls substantiate ₹23.01L delivered with ₹78.39L at L1 stage rather than awarded, and in a separate legal entity. Use the delivered figure (see Underwriting). Measured YOLOv11n at 40 fps on an Artix-7 200T, 3.97M parameters, 263 layers, 80 classes, 24.8 ms latency, at full L2+ ADAS spec. Not simulated. Foundry Muse/GSME MPW contracted, ~$630K shuttle, 79-day fab cycle, 96.7% predicted yield. PrimeSoC feasibility reports and the RTL→GDS physical design plan are filed. Supply chain Manufacturing partners engaged and contracted, EmbeddedIoT (Hyderabad) for PCBA and QFN-128 packaging, Sulakshna for 6-layer automotive PCBs. Far horizon

chunks.section: The option the business buys you, deliberately not funded by this round
chunks.text: SoC4-A is the next-generation part: 1,024 tiles on a finer node, packaged four to a 4U liquid-cooled chassis for 16.76 PFLOPS FP4 peak and ~12 PFLOPS sustained at 1,120 W, with 256 GB of LPDDR5X. The pitch is sovereign AI inference, on-premise compute for Indian and GCC government, telecom and BFSI buyers whose data cannot leave the jurisdiction, plus robotaxi fleet compute and telecom edge. Two reasons it belongs in an investor summary and not in the plan. It is funded from operating profit , not from this round, the model already carries a SoC4 5 nm tapeout programme as an expense line growing to ₹169 Cr by FY2032. And it is the clearest statement of what the company thinks it is: not an ADAS supplier that happens to own a die, but a design team that can aim the same architecture at a different market without starting over. Price it as optionality. SoC2 is the business; this is the option the business buys you.

chunks.section: What a customer actually buys, and what Deepgrid is not selling them
chunks.text: Six use cases carry the commercial plan. Five are regulated functions a truck maker must source; the sixth is the only arena that can transact before qualified silicon exists. The bounding statement Deepgrid sells a bounded camera-perception subsystem inside an accountable integrator’s safety case. It does not own brake actuation, calibration, homologation or warranty, and no use case may be written as if it does. That sentence is the most investor-relevant line in the whole file. It is what makes the Tier-1 sale possible, it caps the liability the company carries, and abandoning it is what would make the sale impossible. Five mandated functions, and when the silicon arrives Four of the five functions bind on one clock, which is the design-in argument: a CV maker must source them together, so a supplier carrying several from one perception core is easier to nominate than four suppliers. And the silicon arrives in the last column, after every mandate date on the chart. The six below carry the commercial plan. The risk: No published ISO 26262 pathway. Until an assessor is engaged, the integrator is comparing a certified incumbent with an uncertified newcomer, and no perception result closes that gap. UC-02 The claim still available is the false alarm, not the detection: The challenge: Four rivals already claim India tuning. India-native is no longer a differentiator. What no competitor has published is a measured nuisance rate, and AIS-162 tests for exactly that. What Deepgrid supplies: The denominator rather than the headline: a scenario-stratified false-positive rate per 1,000 km against a named baseline, on the same silicon class, the same functions and the same test set. Define the India nuisance set, overtaking two-wheelers, cut-in three-wheelers, cattle, roadside encroachment, unlit stationary trucks, wrong-way traffic, kerbside vending Log every trigger and every non-trigger with scenario tags across three paid pilots, with telemetry rights secured in the contract Score false positives per 1,000 km and true-positive recall, stratified by scenario, lighting and monsoon

chunks.section: What a customer actually buys, and what Deepgrid is not selling them
chunks.text: Publish at equal scope; withhold any comparison that silently changes what is being compared Who is in the room: Head of Validation · Tier-1 evaluation engineer · fleet safety manager Organisations: ARAI or ICAT · three paid pilot fleets · the Tier-1 running the evaluation The gate that proves it: One published equal-scope benchmark with scenario-stratified denominators and an independent agency’s protocol. The risk: A nuisance rate without a denominator is marketing. If scenario mix, kilometres and baseline are not fixed in advance, the result will be discounted to zero in a Tier-1 review. UC-03 Two-thirds of India’s road deaths are the road users these two standards were written for: The challenge: Two-wheeler riders were 46.2% of India’s 1,77,175 road deaths in 2024 and pedestrians 20.6%. AIS-186 demands an information signal 15 m before the expected collision point and forbids manual deactivation. What Deepgrid supplies: One India-trained perception core with two output contracts, near-field side and near-field front. Same silicon, same corpus, different detection geometry and signal timing. Side and front near-field cameras into the module; classify pedestrian, adult cyclist and child cyclist Project turn geometry including the counter-turn; raise the signal at least 15 m before the collision point and hold it through the manoeuvre

chunks.section: What a customer actually buys, and what Deepgrid is not selling them
chunks.text: Detect VRUs crossing at 3–5 km/h and cyclists parallel at 0–10 km/h inside the 3.7 m plane; hold through standstill until 15 m past the stopping point Pass the false-information tests, including the traffic-sign case Who is in the room: OEM cab and body engineer · Tier-1 HMI owner · fleet safety officer · driver Organisations: CV OEM · bus body builder · state transport undertaking · ARAI / ICAT The gate that proves it: A characterised near-field result against both test geometries, with the false-information cases run, from an independent agency rather than a bench demo. The risk: The signal cannot be switched off, so a high nuisance rate is permanently in the driver’s peripheral vision. UC-02 is a prerequisite, not a parallel track. UC-04 The only mandated function whose approval evidence is a human-subject study, not a track run: The challenge: Approval is not a track test. The manufacturer must run at least ten participants, none from the development team, in day and night, generating ten or more true-positive or false-negative events, and report per-participant sensitivity. What Deepgrid supplies: An in-cab drowsiness pipeline delivered together with the study that makes it approvable . The differentiator is not the model, it is handing the integrator a completed documentation package instead of a demonstration.

Yet markings on those corridors are worn, inconsistent or absent. What Deepgrid supplies:
