chunks.text: That is why one tapeout can support four revenue lines rather than four separate engineering programmes. **06 · Part one: the revenue plan** First, how volume, price and customer count build to the projection. **07 · Revenue** Revenue is built bottom-up: every line is units multiplied by price. No total is set as a target and back-solved. The plan runs from one point seven crore to eleven hundred and twenty-eight crore across six years, with the inflection in twenty-twenty-eight. **08 · Revenue mix** Road autonomy carries two-thirds of the projection. That concentration is deliberate, because mandated demand is the largest and most predictable pool, but it also means the two truck and mirror ramps are the assumptions that most affect the outcome. **09 · Business mix** Systems, not standalone chip sales, are the economic engine, eighty-three percent of projected revenue. The silicon creates the cost advantage; the revenue is realised by selling complete, certified systems built around it. **10 · Unit economics** Eleven product lines, each priced independently. Prices are held flat across the plan, so growth comes from volume rather than from price increases. The truck kit and the smart mirror together represent seven hundred and twenty crore. **11 · Customers** Accounts grow from five to six hundred and fifty. Average revenue per account peaks in twenty-twenty-nine and then falls as the base broadens into retrofit and fleet channels, which is what removes single-account dependency from the plan. **12 · Part two: margin and profitability** Next, how gross margin expands and overhead ratios decline. **13 · Margin architecture** Each segment carries its own margin path. The blended margin is an output of the mix, not an assumption applied to the top line.

chunks.section: Narration script, DeepGrid Semi financial model walkthrough
chunks.text: The expansion comes from the chip displacing a bought-in module inside every kit. **14 · Profit and loss** Revenue, gross profit and every expense line derive from the same build. Gross margin rises from thirty-nine point seven percent to eighty-seven point four. EBITDA turns positive in twenty-twenty-eight and reaches three hundred and eighty-eight crore by thirty-two. **15 · Operating leverage** The step from loss to structural profitability happens once revenue clears the fixed engineering base. Net margin reaches twenty-four point three percent in the terminal year. **16 · Cost discipline** All three overhead ratios decline as revenue scales. Research and development stays high by design at thirty-three percent, because it carries the next silicon generation rather than only sustaining the current one. **17 · Research investment** About three hundred crore of cumulative research spending funds the next five-nanometre chip from operating profit. Read this correctly: that spending is an expense inside the projections you have seen, not an addition to them. **18 · Part three: silicon and capital** Now what the round funds, what the chip costs, and when it pays back. **19 · Use of funds** Fifty-five crore in total. Silicon takes fifty-four percent, and equals sixty-six percent of the equity round on its own. Working capital sits on the facility, not on equity. **20 · Silicon programme** The tapeout is phased so the largest commitment comes last. Blocks are proven on shared wafers first; the production mask is ordered only once silicon works. Most of the spend is gated on evidence rather than on schedule. **21 · Chip economics** At volume the die costs three dollars eighty-eight, derived from die size, wafer price and yield.

chunks.section: Narration script, DeepGrid Semi financial model walkthrough
chunks.text: The programme recovers its one-time cost at about a hundred and seventy-five thousand chips, well inside the plan horizon. **22 · Schedule risk** If the next-generation chip slips twelve months, the plan loses about fifty-eight crore in the terminal year. The mandated truck and mirror business is unaffected, because it runs on current-generation silicon. **23 · Cash and runway** Cash falls to a low point of ten point one crore in twenty-twenty-nine, then recovers as silicon spending completes and operating profit outpaces working-capital growth. No further equity round is assumed. **24 · Capital structure** Equity funds the asset; debt funds the cycle. Indian commercial-vehicle customers settle in sixty to ninety days, and working capital absorbs eighty crore in the terminal year alone, a cost that should not consume equity. **25 · Ownership and prior capital** The company is founder-controlled, with two point four eight crore of grant and angel capital already deployed. For an incoming investor, governance rights matter more here than the ownership percentage. **26 · Operating plan** Headcount grows from thirty-four to five hundred and forty-one, weighted to engineering. We present it as the operating shape of the plan, and we reconcile it to the expense ratios before close rather than merging the two now. **27 · Part four: risk and decision** Finally, the downside cases and what happens next. **28 · Scenarios** Each case is driven by one revenue multiplier and one overhead adjustment, so the downside is testable rather than asserted.

chunks.section: Narration script, DeepGrid Semi financial model walkthrough
chunks.text: Even on a seventy percent revenue miss, the plan self-funds without a further equity round. **29 · What determines the outcome** Five assumptions carry the projection: the two unit ramps, systems gross margin, yield and wafer cost, working-capital intensity, and the silicon schedule. Against each, we are assembling the evidence a diligence team would ask for. **30 · Close** We are raising forty-five crore to fund working silicon, paired with a ten crore non-dilutive facility, against a plan that reaches self-funding without a further round. We would rather be measured on verifiable gates, working silicon, certification, and paying customers, than on the terminal year.

chunks.section: Narration script, DeepGrid Semi · Product Lines, fifteen SKUs explained
chunks.text: Authored against `storyboard-sku-explainer.md`, not generated from slide text. Every block advances the argument; none of them read the slide aloud. **Arc.** A law created the demand · one 28 nm die serves all fifteen products · here is each one, and what it is downstream of · here is what the portfolio does as a whole · fund the silicon. **Register.** Informative, low pitch, unhurried. 87 blocks, ~3,600 words, roughly 21 minutes. --- **01 · Cover** Fifteen products. One chip. This is the long version, every SKU in the plan, what it physically is, how it runs on shared silicon, who pays for it, and what it contributes. Everything here is a management projection prepared for fundraising. **02 · How to read this deck** Each product gets the same four slides, in the same order: what it is, how it works, who buys it and why now, and how it fits. Four of them get two more, because a working simulator exists and you should watch it rather than take our word. Learn the pattern once and the next eighty slides navigate themselves. **03 · Why now** The demand is legislated, not forecast. Driver-drowsiness, blind-spot and lane-departure obligations land on new and existing commercial vehicles on fixed dates. About a million trucks a year fall in scope. For a fleet operator the question is not whether to buy, it is whose chip is inside when they do. **04 · The move** The whole plan is downstream of one 28 nanometre part, and the programme is deliberately gated. Prove the compute and radar blocks first. Then the full die. Then backend sign-off. The production mask, the largest single commitment, is only paid for once working silicon exists. **05 · The silicon** Here is the part itself.

chunks.section: Narration script, DeepGrid Semi · Product Lines, fifteen SKUs explained
chunks.text: Thirty-two thousand seven hundred and sixty-eight multiply-accumulate units at six hundred megahertz, a hundred and two gigabytes a second of memory bandwidth, hardware softmax, and lockstep cores for the automotive safety path. The number that matters most: it fuses eleven sensor channels in eight point six milliseconds of a thirty-three millisecond frame. Seventy-four percent of the frame is left unused, and that headroom is why one die becomes fifteen products. **06 · The portfolio** All fifteen, ranked by revenue in the final year. Prices are held flat across six years, so growth comes from volume, not from price. Note how far the list ranges, fifty thousand rupees for a mirror unit, eighteen thousand for a bare die, several lakh for a truck kit. Same silicon, priced independently by the market it sells into. **07 · Part one, Road autonomy** Road autonomy is two-thirds of the plan: seven hundred and sixty-two crore, three SKUs. This is where the mandate acts, and where the concentration risk sits. Take these three carefully. **08 · AD0 · What it is** A replacement rear-view mirror with a display built in, four small body cameras and a loom. Fifty thousand rupees, fitted in an afternoon. It is the least sophisticated thing we make and it ships first, on current-generation hardware. **09 · AD0 · How it works** Four cameras cover the quarters a driver cannot see. The chip stitches them into a single surround view and watches the danger zone for anything entering it. The driver gets a stitched image and a directional chime. No braking, no steering, it informs, and that is the whole product. **10 · AD0 · Who buys it** No mandate applies here, which is exactly the point: it already sells on its own merits.

chunks.section: Narration script, DeepGrid Semi · Product Lines, fifteen SKUs explained
chunks.text: Owners and small fleets buy it as an accessory, through fitment shops and accessory catalogues, for visibility and parking. Demand does not wait for a compliance date. **11 · AD0 · How it fits** Two hundred and seventy crore, twenty-four percent of group revenue, at eighty-nine percent gross margin. It carries the highest unit count of anything in the portfolio and the lowest fitment complexity, so it builds the channel reach that the harder products inherit later. **12 · AD1 · What it is** A self-driving retrofit kit for vehicles that never leave a building: a sensor head, a compute box, and a drive-by-wire interface. One lakh rupees. Fitted to forklifts and tugs a site already owns. **13 · AD1 · How it works** This is the first product where the silicon closes the loop instead of advising. Cameras and depth sensing read the aisle, the load and the people in it. The chip localises against a site map it holds onboard. A planner picks a path and a speed. Then drive-by-wire actually steers, accelerates and brakes. The vehicle drives; the driver is not there. **14 · AD1 · Who buys it** Warehouse and industrial operators, direct or through material-handling integrators. Inside a private site no homologation applies, so this is a commercial decision, not a regulatory one, which is why level-four behaviour ships here years before it is legal on a public road. **15 · AD1 · How it fits** Forty-two crore, under four percent of revenue. Small in the model and large in the argument: it is the technical proof point for the road roadmap, running the same silicon in a place where it is allowed to make the decision. **16 · AD1 · Proven in a simulator** We built a drawable warehouse floor for this.

chunks.section: Narration script, DeepGrid Semi · Product Lines, fifteen SKUs explained
chunks.text: You author the route, place workers, peer vehicles, trolleys and spills as obstacles, and run it. The alert policy is configurable, honk, voice, both, silent, because that is a site decision, not ours. And recovery is explicit: it reroutes after a set stuck-time. **17 · AD1 · The simulator, running** Here it is, actually running. Inbound put-away, then a pick run, then the peak-hour floor. Watch the safety ring travelling with the truck and gating its speed, and watch the sensor-fusion panel top right build the bird's-eye view. The third scenario is the one that decides whether a site can run this. **18 · AD2 · What it is** The Smart Truck kit, forward camera, radar, compute box, driver display and the harness that talks to the vehicle. Two and a half lakh rupees. This is the biggest single line in the plan and the one the mandate is written for. **19 · AD2 · How it works** Camera and radar watch the forward path and the blind quarters. The chip fuses both into one object list carrying range and closing speed. Collision, lane and blind-spot logic decide whether to warn. The driver is warned, and where the vehicle supports it, the brake interface is signalled. Radar matters here because closing speed is what a braking decision actually turns on. **20 · AD2 · Who buys it** Fleet operators and truck manufacturers, and the decision is compliance-led rather than discretionary. Retrofit through installers now; factory-fit is the longer, larger route. The buying question is which supplier, on what date. **21 · AD2 · How it fits** Four hundred and fifty crore, forty percent of group revenue from one SKU. That is the concentration to underwrite.

chunks.section: Narration script, DeepGrid Semi · Product Lines, fifteen SKUs explained
chunks.text: It is also why the portfolio has a demand floor at all rather than a demand forecast. **22 · AD2 · Proven in a simulator** Three road profiles, market street, single-carriageway highway, and a deliberate stress test, run against the same perception stack. The vehicle model is real: five hundred and fifty kilograms, two point one metre wheelbase, tyre friction of nought point seven five. Steering angle and lateral acceleration are solved, not scripted. **23 · AD2 · The simulator, running** Watch the planner view in the centre. It redraws from the fused object list, not from an animation path. On the right, the perception rail names what it sees and how far away it is, a motorbike at twenty-six metres, an auto-rickshaw at thirty-eight. Three road profiles, one stack, nothing reloaded between them. **24 · AD2 · G · Sensor coverage** Before we leave the truck kit, look at the sensor layout it actually ships. Two towers retrofit above the existing mirrors, each with a thermal camera, a road camera and a hundred-and-twenty-degree side camera. Two cameras in the cab. Four-D radar front and rear. Watch the coverage cones sweep and overlap, the claim the layout makes is that no quarter of a heavy truck goes unobserved. **25 · Part two, Silicon and compute** Now the half of the business that sells the chip instead of the vehicle. A hundred and ninety-four crore across five SKUs, and the highest margins in the plan, because none of these need an installation crew. **26 · Chipset OEM · What it is** The bare die, in tray or reel, for a customer to place on their own board. Eighteen thousand rupees.

chunks.section: Narration script, DeepGrid Semi · Product Lines, fifteen SKUs explained
chunks.text: No enclosure, no cables, no fitting, we ship silicon and a datasheet, and the customer does the rest. **27 · Chipset OEM · How it works** The customer's own sensors feed their own board. Our die does the perception compute inside their design. Their software decides what to do with the result, and their product ships with our silicon inside it. We supply one stage of someone else's chain. **28 · Chipset OEM · Who buys it** Manufacturers who want Indian-designed silicon and domestic supply rather than an imported part, and who have the engineering to integrate it. Procurement policy is often as decisive as specification here. **29 · Chipset OEM · How it fits** Fifty-four crore at ninety-four percent gross margin, the highest in the portfolio. Every rupee here arrives without installation capacity, warranty logistics or a fitment channel behind it. **30 · Chipset · E · The compute** And this is what the customer is actually buying, running. On the left, the flat eight-by-eight matrix as it works on the FPGA today: sixty-four multiply-accumulates a cycle, iterating the reduction in software. On the right, the cube on twenty-eight nanometre silicon, where that reduction becomes hardware depth and all eight layers fire at once. Watch the tile counters diverge, that gap is the eight-times figure, shown rather than claimed. **31 · A100 one-channel · What it is** The same die on an M.2 module: one camera channel, plus the software kit. Sized to drop into an enclosure and a sensor the customer already owns. **32 · A100 one-channel · How it works** One camera in, one perception stream out, over a standard module interface.

chunks.section: Narration script, DeepGrid Semi · Product Lines, fifteen SKUs explained
chunks.text: It is the smallest configuration the part supports, and the point is that it is the same part, running less. **33 · A100 one-channel · Who buys it** Product teams who want the silicon and the toolchain but do not want to design a board around a bare die. It converts a semiconductor sale into a module sale for customers without a hardware team. **34 · A100 one-channel · How it fits** Twenty-five and a half crore, at eighty-nine percent margin. Modest on its own; it exists to make the silicon reachable by customers who would otherwise not buy at all. **35 · A100 two-channel · What it is** A board-level module with two camera inputs and the software kit. Twenty-five thousand rupees, the middle rung of the compute-box ladder, and the one that sells in the largest numbers of the three. **36 · A100 two-channel · How it works** Two channels is where fusion begins to matter, the moment you have to reconcile two views of the same scene into one object list. It is the first configuration that justifies purpose-built transformer hardware over a general-purpose processor. **37 · A100 two-channel · Who buys it** Systems that need more than a single view but not full surround coverage, reversing with side detection, a two-camera inspection rig, a small autonomous platform. Buyers who would find a four-channel card wasteful and a single channel insufficient. **38 · A100 two-channel · How it fits** Twenty-eight point eight crore. A step on a ladder rather than a destination, but the ladder is what lets one die address several price points at once. **39 · A100 four-channel · What it is** A PCIe card carrying the chip with four camera inputs, for a host system that provides the enclosure and the power.

chunks.section: Narration script, DeepGrid Semi · Product Lines, fifteen SKUs explained
chunks.text: Fifty thousand rupees, and the largest configuration we sell as a component. **40 · A100 four-channel · How it works** Four channels demands the memory bandwidth the compute geometry was designed around. Each compute cube runs its own local memory access against a banked cache, which is what keeps utilisation high instead of starving on a single shared path. This is the configuration that shows why the die is built the way it is. **41 · A100 four-channel · Who buys it** Customers building full surround perception who want the compute inside their own architecture rather than in a box we supply, robotics platforms, industrial vehicles, and anyone who already has a host machine and needs to add sight to it. **42 · A100 four-channel · How it fits** Thirty-six crore, the largest of the three compute boxes. Together the A100 family is ninety crore of revenue that needs no vehicle, no installer and no homologation. **43 · T100 licence · What it is** Not hardware at all. A licence to the trained perception models and the toolchain, so a customer can run our software on their own platform. Priced per deployment, with nothing shipped in a box. **44 · T100 licence · How it works** The models are the accumulated result of running these sensors on Indian roads. A customer licences that, integrates it, and ships. There is no board, no bill of materials, and nothing to manufacture. **45 · T100 licence · Who buys it** Teams that want perception tuned for Indian road conditions, the traffic mix, the lane discipline, the light, without spending three years collecting the data to train it themselves.

chunks.section: Narration script, DeepGrid Semi · Product Lines, fifteen SKUs explained
chunks.text: The dataset is the product here, not the code. **46 · T100 licence · How it fits** Fifty crore at ninety-four percent margin, and it starts later than everything else, in the 2029 financial year, because a licence needs a track record before anyone buys one. It is the only line in the plan with no bill of materials whatsoever. **47 · Part three, Fleet and mobility** Two SKUs, eighty-nine crore, and the highest revenue per unit anywhere in the portfolio. Here we stop selling a product and start selling the work the product does. **48 · TaaS · What it is** Not a sale. A vehicle we own and operate under contract, where the customer pays for the transport rather than the truck. The revenue per unit is the largest in the plan because we are booking the whole job. **49 · TaaS · How it works** The vehicle runs the same autonomy stack as the kit we sell. Fleet logic schedules it, routes it, and hands off to a remote operator when the situation exceeds what the vehicle should decide alone. The difference from AD2 is commercial, not technical. **50 · TaaS · Who buys it** Operators comparing cost per tonne-kilometre against a driven alternative, and increasingly comparing against driver availability rather than driver cost, because on many routes the constraint is finding a driver at all. **51 · TaaS · How it fits** Sixty-six crore. It is the line that shows what the technology is worth when we capture the operating margin instead of the hardware margin. It also carries operational risk the product lines do not: we own the asset and the uptime. **52 · Seaport AGV · What it is** An autonomous container-yard vehicle working inside a port perimeter.

chunks.section: Narration script, DeepGrid Semi · Product Lines, fifteen SKUs explained
chunks.text: A controlled site, but not an easy one: heavy equipment overhead, tight lanes between stacks, and real consequences for a positioning error. **53 · Seaport AGV · How it works** Under a quay crane, satellite positioning degrades exactly where precision matters most. Sensor fusion on our silicon holds seven centimetres in the open and twenty-two under the crane, where satellite alone falls away. That positioning is what makes crane-synchronised dispatch possible at all. **54 · Seaport AGV · Who buys it** Terminal operators, measured on throughput and labour cost inside a geofenced site. No public-road homologation applies, so adoption is limited by operational confidence rather than regulation. **55 · Seaport AGV · How it fits** Twenty-two and a half crore. Read its market share differently from the others: the sized pool is total port automation including cranes and software, and we sell only the vehicle layer. **56 · Seaport AGV · Proven in a simulator** A working twin of a container terminal, built to prove the three things the programme asks for: that positioning holds where satellite fails, that routing copes with congestion, and that scheduling collapses crane idle time. It runs in shadow mode first, advising the terminal before it is given control. **57 · Seaport AGV · The simulator, running** Quay discharge, then the container canyon, then peak mixed traffic. Watch the two confidence bars diverge as the vehicle enters the canyon, satellite drops, fusion holds. The trial panel on the right carries the numbers: seven centimetres open, twenty-two under crane, nine percent error on arrival time. **58 · Part four, Sensors and robotics** Five SKUs, eighty-three and a half crore.

chunks.section: Narration script, DeepGrid Semi · Product Lines, fifteen SKUs explained
chunks.text: Two purposes: sensors that make the main products work in conditions where cameras fail, and robotics platforms that put the same silicon into a second market cycle. **59 · Thermal camera · What it is** A bolt-on long-wave infrared pod with its own lens and heater, feeding the compute box. Forty thousand rupees. It is an accessory to the systems above it, not a standalone product. **60 · Thermal camera · How it works** It reads emitted heat rather than reflected light, so a person or an animal separates from the background in the dark, through glare, dust and smoke. The chip runs detection on the thermal image alongside the visible one. This is the channel that keeps working when the others stop. **61 · Thermal camera · Who buys it** Fleets running at night and through the monsoon, where camera-only detection degrades sharply. It is sold as an upgrade to a system already fitted, which makes it a second sale into an existing customer rather than a new acquisition. **62 · Thermal camera · How it fits** Sixteen crore at fifty percent gross margin, half the group average, because a sensor carries real component cost. Its job is to raise the capability of the products around it, not to carry the plan. **63 · 4D radar · What it is** A sealed radar pod, mounted forward or on a corner, feeding the same compute box. Twenty-five thousand rupees, and weatherproof by design because it has to work in the conditions that defeat everything else. **64 · 4D radar · How it works** It illuminates the scene and reads the returns, and the radar block on the die turns those returns into range, velocity and angle. Tracks are held across frames, including through rain and dust.

chunks.section: Narration script, DeepGrid Semi · Product Lines, fifteen SKUs explained
chunks.text: Radar supplies closing speed, the one quantity a camera estimates and a radar measures. **65 · 4D radar · Who buys it** Operations where weather and dust defeat cameras, and any application where a braking decision has to be defensible afterwards, because a measured closing speed stands up where an estimated one does not. **66 · 4D radar · How it fits** Seven and a half crore, the smallest line in the plan. It is here because the flagship product needs it, not because it is a business on its own. **67 · H100 wearable · What it is** A wrist-worn band with on-body sensors and a radio link to the vehicle. Fifteen hundred rupees. It is driver monitoring without a camera pointed at the driver's face, the same obligation, answered a different way. **68 · H100 wearable · How it works** The band reads pulse and movement continuously, the vehicle correlates that with how the vehicle is being driven, and fatigue is flagged before it becomes a lane departure. It measures the driver directly rather than inferring from the road. **69 · H100 wearable · Who buys it** Fleets meeting driver-drowsiness obligations that want a lower-intrusion option than an in-cab camera. Driver acceptance is a genuine adoption factor, and a wristband clears it more easily. **70 · H100 wearable · How it fits** Ten crore at fifty percent margin. A hedge on how the drowsiness requirement is satisfied in practice, on a portfolio that otherwise answers it with a camera. **71 · D-HUMR · What it is** An unmanned ground vehicle for defence logistics and reconnaissance. It is the only line in the portfolio selling to a government customer, and the only one whose buying cycle is measured in years rather than quarters. **72 · D-HUMR · How it works** The same fusion stack, pointed outward instead of forward.

chunks.section: Narration script, DeepGrid Semi · Product Lines, fifteen SKUs explained
chunks.text: Radar, thermal and camera tracks along a perimeter are classified individually, then correlated, so a vehicle loitering on an access road and a person approaching the fence stop being two unrelated contacts. **73 · D-HUMR · Who buys it** Defence procurement, for tasks where sending a vehicle is preferable to sending people. Qualification is long and the cycles are slow, but once a platform is in, it is very hard to displace. **74 · D-HUMR · How it fits** Thirty crore at sixty-eight percent margin. Its real value is strategic: a sovereign customer, a separate procurement route, and a use case that does not depend on the automotive mandate at all. **75 · D-HUMR · Proven in a simulator** A live perimeter console. It correlates a vehicle track with a human track into one threat, escalates it along a timed ladder from loiter to approach to breach risk, and hands the target to ground sensors, a patrol drone or a sea buoy. The feature that matters is the restraint: benign tracks are held and never escalated, because false-alarm rate is what gets a perimeter system switched off. **76 · D-HUMR · The simulator, running** Coordinated intrusion, then perimeter patrol, then a maritime approach. Watch two separate tracks fuse into one threat, and watch the escalation ladder on the right fill in, the operator sees intent forming rather than an alarm at the breach. The console states its reasoning in words. **77 · D100 drone · What it is** A flight-capable compute and perception kit sold to airframe builders. It is the smallest and lightest configuration of the same silicon, constrained by weight and power rather than by cost. **78 · D100 drone · How it works** Cameras and an inertial unit read the scene and the airframe's own motion.

chunks.section: Narration script, DeepGrid Semi · Product Lines, fifteen SKUs explained
chunks.text: The chip holds position and detects obstacles onboard, so the aircraft is not dependent on a radio link to stay safe. The flight controller executes. **79 · D100 drone · Who buys it** Airframe builders with onboard autonomy requirements, inspection, survey, and any mission flown where the radio link cannot be relied upon. They buy compute, not aircraft, and they build the rest themselves. **80 · D100 drone · How it fits** Twenty crore. Treat it as optionality rather than base case: the same die, in a market with a different cycle and different buyers, entered without designing new silicon to get there. **81 · Part five, Portfolio economics** Fifteen products explained. Now what they do together, concentration, timing, where the autonomy actually runs, where the margin is, and how much of each market we are assuming we win. **82 · Concentration** Be clear about this: two SKUs carry sixty-four percent. The truck kit and the smart mirror are the same product family sold to overlapping buyers, so a certification delay or an installation bottleneck hits seven hundred and twenty crore at once, more than the other thirteen SKUs combined. That is the single largest risk in the plan. **83 · Sequencing** Six SKUs earn revenue in the 2027 financial year, nine more in 2028. The 2027 revenue is one point seven crore across six products, on current-generation hardware, deliberately small. The ramp switches on when production silicon reaches market, and the licence line starts later still. The shape of this plan is gated by the chip, which is what the round funds. **84 · Where autonomy runs** Eighty-six percent of revenue runs outdoors, where public-road rules and homologation apply. Six percent runs indoors, geofenced, where level four ships years earlier on identical silicon.

chunks.section: Narration script, DeepGrid Semi · Product Lines, fifteen SKUs explained
chunks.text: Eight percent is pure compute with no vehicle exposure at all. Same chip, three very different regulatory positions. **85 · Margin** Volume and margin sit in different places, and that is the useful thing on this slide. Systems are eighty-three percent of revenue, so group economics track systems. But the marginal rupee is worth most in semiconductors at ninety-four percent, and those lines need no installation capacity. Growth in the silicon SKUs improves group margin without adding operational load. **86 · Headroom** No SKU in this plan assumes we win its market. Every line sits under two percent of its own sized demand pool, and most pools are global while our addressable market is the India slice, so the real share is higher than shown. Read the port line differently: that pool is total port automation, and we sell only the vehicle layer. **87 · The ask** Fifteen products, one tapeout. The demand is legislated, the margin sits in silicon that needs no installation capacity, and no line in the plan requires us to win its market. Release the capital against silicon, certification and paying customers, not against the forecast. The portfolio is not fifteen bets. It is one bet, fifteen times over.

India Edition India Edition Sterling Tools partners MINIEYE to accelerate ADAS and Driver Monitoring Solutions for India 4 min read·Published on Jan 19, 2026 · 6:25 AM IST·Updated Jul 14, 2026 · 12:37 PM IST Listen to this article Speed1.0x -Advertisement- Sterling Tools Limited (BSE: 530759 \| NSE: STERTOOLS), a leading automotive components and technology manufacturer, has partnered with MINIEYE, a China-based intelligent driving and in-cabin solutions provider listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, to accelerate the deployment of Advanced Driver Assistance Systems and Driver Monitoring Systems tailored specifically for the Indian automotive market. The partnership is focused on adapting intelligent driving technologies to India’s unique and highly complex road environment. As part of the collaboration, Sterling Tools will support perception tuning and on-ground industry engagement, enabling ADAS and driver monitoring systems to be trained for India-specific road scenarios, mixed traffic conditions, and diverse driving patterns. This approach recognises that intelligent driving systems require deep data-driven perception development and application-level engineering to operate reliably in Indian conditions, rather than being direct replications of solutions deployed in global markets. The collaboration centres on application engineering and system adaptation to ensure that ADAS and driver monitoring technologies align with Indian driving environments, road infrastructure, and real-world operating conditions. The development effort will cover both passenger vehicles and commercial vehicles, supporting OEMs with solutions that are engineered for local requirements while meeting regulatory and safety expectations.

As part of this initiative, the adapted systems will include technologies such as Autonomous Emergency Braking, Forward Collision Warning, Lane Departure Warning Systems, Driver Drowsiness and Attention Warning Systems, Blind Spot Monitoring, and other advanced safety functions. These systems will be aligned with OEM requirements and evolving regulatory frameworks, ensuring readiness for large-scale adoption across vehicle segments. India’s automotive industry is entering a critical safety transition phase, with mandatory fitment of ADAS and Driver Drowsiness and Attention Warning Systems in new vehicle models scheduled to take effect from January 1, 2027. As adoption accelerates, OEMs are increasingly seeking safety technologies that are engineered specifically for Indian traffic behaviour, road complexity, and operating conditions, while remaining fully compliant with regulatory mandates. MINIEYE brings extensive global experience in intelligent driving and in-cabin technologies to the partnership. Its solutions are compliant with the EU General Safety Regulation and supported by Automotive SPICE V4.0 CL3 certification. The company’s systems are already deployed across international markets including Europe, the UK, Australia, Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and South America, providing a strong foundation for scalable, regulation-ready deployments in India. -Advertisement- \\ **Sterling Tools Q4 Results: Net profit falls 82% YoY Rs 1.59 crore, revenue up 11%** \\ \\ \\ **Sterling Tools’ subsidiary signs Technology License and Supply agreements with China’s Landworld for EV chargers** \\ \\ \\ **Sterling Tools joins forces with China’s Meishuo Electric to enhance power transmission in India** \\ \\ RejectAccept

India's commercial vehicle market presents a distinct set of requirements for ADAS deployment. Delivering reliable perception at scale requires software capable of running on low-cost, resource-constrained hardware while maintaining stable performance across diverse and high-density traffic conditions. For commercial vehicle operators, where uptime and operating efficiency are central concerns, both technical performance and deployment economics must be addressed. SVNet is designed to meet these requirements. The software delivers stable object detection and classification across the road conditions characteristic of the Indian market, including mixed-traffic environments with two- and three-wheelers, pedestrians, and other vulnerable road users, while operating within the compute budgets suited to commercial-vehicle platforms. This enables OEMs to deploy core ADAS functions, including automatic emergency braking, forward collision warning, and lane departure warning, across multiple vehicle models and configurations from a single software stack. The program is structured for deployment across multiple vehicle models, enabling the OEM to standardize a single perception platform while adapting to model-specific hardware configurations. With approximately five million cumulative SVNet units deployed globally, STRADVISION brings the production scale and software maturity that high-volume commercial programs require. Philip Vidal, CBO of STRADVISION, said, "India's commercial vehicle segment is one of the most consequential ADAS markets opening right now. The scale of the fleet, the complexity of the traffic environment, and the cost requirements make it a genuine test of whether perception software can perform where it matters most.

SVNet was built for exactly this kind of deployment, and this program is a strong validation of that." This development reflects a broader shift in the automotive industry, where the focus of ADAS competition is expanding from performance to efficiency and scalability. STRADVISION will continue to support OEMs with perception solutions that can be applied across diverse vehicle platforms and market conditions. **About STRADVISION** Founded in 2014, STRADVISION is an automotive industry pioneer in artificial intelligence-based vision perception technology for vehicles. The company is accelerating the advent of fully autonomous vehicles by making Autonomous Driving and ADAS features available at a fraction of the market cost compared with competitors. STRADVISION's SVNet is being deployed on various vehicle models in partnership with OEMs; can power ADAS and autonomous vehicles worldwide; and is serviced by over 300 employees in Seoul, San Jose, Detroit, Tokyo, Shanghai, and Dusseldorf. STRADVISION has been honored with Frost & Sullivan's 2022 Global Technology Innovation Leadership Award, the Gold Award at the 2022 and 2021 AutoSens Awards for Best-in-Class Software for Perception Systems, the 2020 Autonomous Vehicle Technology ACES Award in Autonomy (software category), and 2025 Top SME Innovator by CLEPA for Breakthrough AI 3D Perception Network Technology. In addition, STRADVISION and its software have achieved TISAX's AL3 standard for information security management, as well as being certified to the ISO 9001:2015 for Quality Management Systems and ISO 26262 for Automotive Functional Safety. chunks.section: ZF Commercial Vehicle Control Systems India Limited
chunks.text: Secures an ADAS Business Nomination from an Indian E-Mobility CV OEM • ZF CVCS secures business nomination for ADAS development across multiple electric vehicle platforms, including 13.5-meter coaches, 55- ton trucks and 7m, 9m, and 12m buses. • ZF’s ADAS solution, equipped with ZF’s OnGuardMAX and short-range radar technology, offers a wide-ranging set of 16 advanced features including AEBS, BSIS, DDAWS, LDWS, MOIS etc • The solution ensures full compliance with the upcoming Indian safety regulation. (GSR 184e) • Validated over 300,000 km under diverse Indian road conditions, reinforcing reliability and performance. <u>Chennai, India, December 3, 2025</u>- ZF Commercial Vehicle Control Systems India Limited (CVCS) has secured business nomination from a leading E-Mobility CV OEM in India to develop and calibrate an Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) suite tailored to the upcoming Indian safety regulation (GSR 184e). This ZF solution is market-ready for India and is certified by the Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI) for full compliance with the upcoming Indian safety regulation (GSR 184e). Developed for scalability, the solution supports SAE Level 2 automation and is designed to enable higher automation levels for global applications, while addressing the unique and current challenges of Indian road conditions.

chunks.section: ZF Commercial Vehicle Control Systems India Limited
chunks.text: This business nomination includes key ADAS components and systems designed for coaches, heavy-duty trucks, and tractor-trailers, ensuring robust performance across diverse commercial vehicle platforms. **ZF Group** Global Corporate & Marketing Communications 88038 Friedrichshafen Deutschland · Germany press.zf.com --- Akash Passey, Chairman (Non-Executive Director), ZF Commercial Vehicle Control Systems India Limited added that “ZF Group’s commitment to safety and sustainability is seen in its products designed to address the ADAS regulatory framework in India. Our solutions are compliant and have also been proven under real-world conditions. As the country moves towards increasing automation and enhanced safety standards, we are ready with future-ready technologies that address the expectations of our OEM partners.” Paramjit Singh Chadha, Managing Director, ZF Commercial Vehicle Control Systems India Limited stated that “At ZF CVCS, our ADAS solutions are designed to enhance safety, reduce fatigue and support better decision-making. By ensuring that advanced safety systems more accessible and intuitive, we are helping drivers drive with greater confidence and comfort. This nomination reinforces our commitment to inclusive innovation and safer roads for everyone.”

chunks.section: Key Highlights of ZF’s ADAS Systems
chunks.text: • Proven Performance: Validated over 300,000 km on Indian roads and 65,000km in collaboration with customers, ensuring reliability in real-world conditions. • Regulatory Compliance: Fully compliant with Indian homologation standards, including o AIS-162 - Advanced Emergency Braking Systems (AEBS) o AIS-184 - Driver Drowsiness and Attention Warning Systems (DDAW) o AIS-186 - Blind Spot Information System for the Detection of Bicycles (BSIS) o AIS-187 - Moving Off Information System for the Detection of Pedestrians and Cyclists (MOIS) o AIS-188 - Lane Departure Warning System (LDWS) • Feature-Rich Suite: This ADAS solution, equipped with ZF’s OnGuardMAX and short-range radar technology, offers a **ZF Group** Global Corporate & Marketing Communications comprehensive set of 16 advanced features, including AEB, BSIS, DDAW, LDWS, MOIS. Bringing together global expertise and local validation, ZF delivers ADAS solutions that meet stringent regulations and future automation needs. With its globally proven reliability, inclusive design and a commitment to safer roads, ZF is driving India toward smarter, safer and sustainable transportation - Redefining India’s Mobility. Press contact: Mallika Apte, Head, Corporate Communications and PR, ZF Group India Phone: +91 914 500 3565, email <u>mallika.apte@zf.com</u>

ZF is a global technology company supplying advanced mobility products and systems for passenger cars, commercial vehicles and industrial technology. Its comprehensive product range is primarily aimed at vehicle manufacturers, mobility providers and start-up companies in the fields of transportation and mobility. ZF electrifies a wide range of vehicle types. With its products, the company contributes to reducing emissions, protecting the climate as well as enhancing safe mobility. Alongside the automotive sector – passenger cars and commercial vehicles – ZF also serves market segments such as construction and agricultural machinery, wind power, marine propulsion, rail drives and test systems. With some 161,600 employees worldwide, ZF reported sales of €41.4 billion in fiscal 2024. The company operates 161 production locations in 30 countries. For further press information and photos, please visit: www.zf.com

ZF’s Commercial Vehicle Solutions (CVS) division is shaping the future of commercial transportation ecosystems. ZF’s CVS division makes commercial vehicles safer, smarter and sustainable to achieve the vision of zero accidents and zero emissions. With its comprehensive technology portfolio, ZF CVS offers tailored solutions for every step of an OEM and fleets’ transformation journey, helping solve complex problems while creating long term value. ZF CVS’s unique capability to digitalize commercial vehicle systems solutions and enhance vehicle intelligence is paving the way towards the commercial vehicle of the future. ZF CVS unites ZF’s former Commercial Vehicle Technology and Commercial Vehicle Control Systems divisions, the latter being formed following ZF’s acquisition of WABCO in Spring 2020. <!-- converted from icp-and-gtm-strategy-jul-2026.docx --> Strategic Go-To-Market and Ideal Customer Profile Framework for DeepGrid Semi: Navigating the Pre-Series A Transition to Custom Silicon in India and the GCC

chunks.section: Executive Summary: The Pre-Series A Strategic Crossroads
chunks.text: The commercial autonomous vehicle (AV) and advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) semiconductor market is characterized by structural capital intensity, prolonged design-in validation cycles, and significant cash burn before achieving commercial viability1. Within this high-barrier landscape, DeepGrid Semi, currently incubated at T-Hub Phase 2 in Hyderabad, stands at a critical technological and commercial crossroads1. As an early-stage, pre-revenue fabless semiconductor startup, DeepGrid has successfully validated its custom INT8 edge-AI architecture on Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs)1. However, the enterprise currently lacks established Tier-1 automotive customers or the massive capital required to transition from high-cost FPGA prototyping, which currently costs approximately () per board, to mass-produced custom Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs), projected to cost less than () per chip at scale1. To fund the physical fabrication of its custom combo-die, DeepGrid is actively seeking to raise a () Pre-Series A venture capital round1. For institutional investors, technical validation on FPGAs is insufficient; the primary investment thesis depends on demonstrating a realistic, rapid path to commercial traction and cash-flow generation1. This report establishes a systematic framework for identifying DeepGrid’s Ideal Customer Profiles (ICPs) and maps out actionable Go-To-Market (GTM) strategies customized to these profiles1.

chunks.section: Executive Summary: The Pre-Series A Strategic Crossroads
chunks.text: By analyzing the commercial playbooks of global autonomous vehicle leaders and domestic Indian semiconductor startups, this report outlines how DeepGrid can leverage near-term regulatory safety mandates, dual-use tactical contracts, and unique hardware price advantages to bypass traditional multi-year automotive OEM cycles, mitigate capital burn, and build a highly defensible, localized data moat in India and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) markets1.

chunks.section: Systematic Methodology for Identifying DeepGrid’s ICP
chunks.text: A common point of failure for fabless semiconductor startups is targeting broad, unconstrained market segments without evaluating customer buying behaviors, technical integration friction, and regulatory timelines1. To optimize its limited Pre-Series A capital, DeepGrid must utilize a rigorous, multi-dimensional diagnostic framework to identify, score, and prioritize potential customer segments1. The systematic methodology relies on five critical strategic evaluation dimensions: Regulatory Compulsion Index: This dimension measures whether the customer's purchase is discretionary or driven by immediate, non-discretionary legislative mandates1. Segments facing hard regulatory compliance deadlines (such as India's upcoming heavy vehicle safety standards or Saudi Arabia's tracking laws) are prioritized because they exhibit condensed sales cycles and low marketing friction4. Technical Integration & Certification Friction: This parameter evaluates the engineering hours, architectural modifications, and safety homologation testing (such as ISO 26262 functional safety, AIS-004 electromagnetic compatibility, and AIS-189 cybersecurity certifications) required to design DeepGrid's silicon into the customer's platform7. Higher integration complexity delays time-to-revenue and increases cash burn1. Price Elasticity & BOM Limit: This dimension analyzes the customer's tolerance for hardware acquisition costs1. Large commercial transport fleets and logistics networks in emerging markets exhibit extreme price sensitivity and thin operational margins, making them highly receptive to DeepGrid's projected low-cost ASIC board Bill of Materials (BOM) of , compared to expensive foreign imported computing systems costing upwards of 1.

chunks.section: Systematic Methodology for Identifying DeepGrid’s ICP
chunks.text: Sales Cycle & Time-to-Revenue Duration: This metric measures the duration between initial technical engagement and commercial volume shipments1. Direct passenger vehicle OEM sales cycles typically span three to five years, whereas off-highway industrial projects or defense research contracts often finalize procurement in under six to twelve months1. Operational Design Domain (ODD) Entropy: This dimension maps the physical environments of the application, contrasting highly structured, predictable interstate highways with unstructured, chaotic urban roadways and off-highway terrains1. High-entropy environments require real-world, localized training datasets that can process unique local variables (such as three-wheelers, unlit vehicles, and wandering livestock), which provides a natural moat against general-purpose global computing platforms1. chunks.section: Detailed Evaluation of the Three ICP Strategic Options
chunks.text: The systematic application of the diagnostic framework reveals three viable, distinct strategic options for DeepGrid's customer targeting1. Each option presents unique operating environments, technical requirements, and strategic entry points1. Option A: Tactical Defense and Constrained Off-Highway Environments Option A targets tactical military unmanned systems, national security agencies, and heavy off-highway industrial operators, such as seaports, mining terminals, and enclosed manufacturing campuses1. ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ ICP OPTION A: TACTICAL DEFENSE & OFF-HIGHWAY │ ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ • Targets: Unmanned Ground Vehicles, Port AGVs, Campus AMRs. │ │ • Primary Pain Point: Lack of secure, localized, low-latency compute.│ │ • Key Silicon Enabler: D100 lockstep secure RISC-V enclave. │ │ • Buying Behavior: Insensitive to cost; demands high IP sovereignty.│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ The underlying buying behavior in this segment is driven by a critical need for secure, localized computing hardware that operates reliably in high-entropy, GPS-denied environments without relying on external cloud communications1. National defense agencies require absolute intellectual property sovereignty and hardware-level cybersecurity to prevent external jamming or unauthorized system overrides1. In this context, DeepGrid's inclusion of the D100 lockstep secure RISC-V enclave directly addresses these national defense specifications, providing an isolated cryptographic execution environment for tactical Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs) and automated logistical systems1.

chunks.section: Detailed Evaluation of the Three ICP Strategic Options
chunks.text: This buying profile is highly insensitive to upfront hardware costs but demands military-grade physical system hardening, wide thermal operating tolerances, and direct access to raw sensory processing engines1. In the industrial off-highway sub-segment, such as automated guided vehicles (AGVs) operating in major commercial seaports, the customer's pain point is operational efficiency and collision mitigation within tightly constrained spatial zones1. This profile is highly receptive to the direct integration of the R100 radar DSP and the T100 thermal/LiDAR DSP on a single silicon die, which eliminates the latency and physical reliability issues associated with multi-chip board configurations on heavy industrial machinery1.

chunks.section: Detailed Evaluation of the Three ICP Strategic Options
chunks.text: Option B: Non-Discretionary Aftermarket Commercial Fleet Retrofit Option B targets the massive, highly fragmented commercial aftermarket transport sector, specifically focusing on private logistics operators, intercity transport fleets, and bulk cargo distribution companies managing medium and heavy commercial vehicles ( and categories)1. ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ ICP OPTION B: AFTERMARKET FLEET RETROFIT │ ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ • Targets: N2/N3 commercial vehicle operators, private cargo fleets.│ │ • Primary Pain Point: Legal mandate compliance vs. high system cost.│ │ • Key Silicon Enabler: Low-cost A100 AI processor & R100 Radar DSP.│ │ • Buying Behavior: Highly cost-sensitive; requires rapid payback. │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ These buyers face immediate, non-discretionary regulatory pressure from national ministries of transport to implement advanced driver assistance technologies to curb road fatalities1. However, these operators run on razor-thin operating margins and cannot afford to retire their existing vehicle fleets to purchase new, factory-compliant models14. Consequently, their primary buying criterion is the availability of low-cost, homologated, retroactive safety packages that can be installed on existing trucks to achieve legal compliance without causing significant business disruption1. This customer profile displays extreme price sensitivity1. When evaluating safety upgrades, these operators compare the cost of compliance against the financial penalties of non-compliance and rising commercial insurance premiums2.

chunks.section: Detailed Evaluation of the Three ICP Strategic Options
chunks.text: Traditional imported ADAS solutions, which rely on premium merchant silicon platforms, cost upwards of to per commercial vehicle, making them economically unviable for the majority of emerging market fleet operators1. DeepGrid's custom silicon design allows it to deliver a complete, dual-sensor retroactive kit at an estimated price point of to , directly resolving the customer's financial constraints1. Furthermore, because these fleets operate continuously in highly unstructured mixed traffic containing three-wheelers, pedestrians, and unmarked roadways, these operators require a system optimized to eliminate false positives in local road conditions1. DeepGrid's custom 3D Systolic Tensor Cube microarchitecture is specifically engineered to run localized perception models at high framerates on mature silicon, providing superior real-world reliability in unstructured traffic compared to general-purpose Western computing boards1.

chunks.section: Detailed Evaluation of the Three ICP Strategic Options
chunks.text: Option C: Sovereign Compliance and OEM Factory Line-Fit Embedding Option C targets domestic medium and heavy commercial vehicle manufacturers (OEMs) producing passenger buses () and freight trucks () in India and emerging automotive assembly hubs in the GCC1. ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ ICP OPTION C: OEM FACTORY LINE-FIT │ ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ • Targets: Domestic Indian and GCC commercial vehicle OEMs [cite: 1, 20].│ │ • Primary Pain Point: Platform BOM inflation and supply vulnerabilities.│ │ • Key Silicon Enabler: Single-die integration of 6 modular chiplets. │ │ • Buying Behavior: Long-term validation; highly conservative; Tier-1 focus.│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ These OEMs are highly conservative, structurally risk-averse buyers operating on long development horizons1. Their buying decisions are governed by strict safety compliance, supply chain continuity, and platform-level bill of materials optimization1. The primary pain point for these manufacturers is the rising cost of electronics and software complexity7. Integrating a suite of mandatory safety systems, including advanced emergency braking, blind spot monitoring, lane departure warnings, and driver drowsiness alerts, typically requires mounting multiple separate electronic control units (ECUs), sensor processors, and CAN gateways from different Tier-1 suppliers, which inflates the vehicle's manufacturing BOM and creates complex software integration bottlenecks1.

chunks.section: Detailed Evaluation of the Three ICP Strategic Options
chunks.text: OEM buyers are highly receptive to DeepGrid's single-die, six-chiplet system-on-chip architecture, which consolidates AI processing (A100), radar DSP (R100), secure computing (D100), and vehicle gateway telematics (S100) onto a single silicon substrate1. This level of integration eliminates multi-chip board complexity, reduces the physical footprint within the vehicle's electrical cabinet, and lowers the vehicle's platform manufacturing cost1. However, because these buyers will not purchase directly from an unproven, pre-revenue startup, they require DeepGrid to integrate with their preferred, established Tier-1 automotive component suppliers1. These Tier-1 channel partners act as the interface, absorbing physical assembly, long-term product warranties, and vehicle integration liabilities1.

chunks.section: Competitive Positioning Matrix of Autonomy and Silicon Competitors
chunks.text: The global autonomous vehicle and edge semiconductor markets contain both large, well-capitalized Western incumbents and specialized, nimble domestic Indian startups1. Understanding the technical choices, pricing models, and strategic milestones of these competitors is essential to validating DeepGrid’s unique positioning for institutional venture capital investors1. The matrix below provides a detailed technical and commercial comparison of global and domestic players:

chunks.section: Tailored Go-To-Market Strategies Mapped to ICP Options
chunks.text: To maximize commercial execution while managing capital limitations, DeepGrid must implement distinct, sequentially structured GTM roadmaps specifically designed around the buying habits of each prioritized ICP option1. ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ ICP OPTIONS MAPPED TO GTM STRATEGY PHASING │ ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ │ │ [ OPTION A: TACTICAL WEDGE ] ──────────────────────► Months 0 - 6 │ │ • Deploy FPGA-based prototypes directly to defense UGVs & port AGVs │ │ • Generate immediate non-dilutive contract cash-flow │ │ │ │ [ OPTION B: AFTERMARKET RETROFIT ] ────────────────► Months 6 - 18 │ │ • Leverage Indian DLI Scheme for TSMC 28nm MPW tape-out │ │ • Distribute low-cost homologated safety kits to private N2/N3 fleets │ │ │ │ [ OPTION C: TIER-1 / OEM INTEGRATION ] ────────────► Months 18 - 36 │ │ • Partner with domestic Tier-1 auto-component suppliers │ │ • Design standard factory line-fit ASIC ECUs directly to major OEMs │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ GTM Strategy for ICP Option A: The Tactical and Off-Highway Wedge (Months 0–6) The near-term objective of Option A is to generate immediate cash flow, accumulate real-world operational testing metrics, and establish early credibility with venture capitalists without waiting for physical ASIC fabrication1. Direct FPGA Field Deployment: DeepGrid must bypass automotive OEM validation queues by deploying its fully functional, FPGA-based development boards directly into constrained off-highway environments1. These platforms run the core 3D Systolic Tensor Cube perception models at standard framerates, proving algorithmic efficacy in the real world1.

chunks.section: Tailored Go-To-Market Strategies Mapped to ICP Options
chunks.text: Tactical Defense Procurement: The startup must actively target the Indian defense establishment's tactical UGV, drone, and border security modernization initiatives1. By integrating the lockstep RISC-V secure enclave (D100) directly on the FPGA board, DeepGrid can bid on sovereign-compliance research and development contracts1. This wedge has already demonstrated commercial viability, securing in defense contract revenue1. Constrained Campus AGV Pilots: DeepGrid must implement proof-of-concept deployments with regional seaports and industrial campuses to automate heavy cargo-handling equipment1. These closed environments operate under low speed limits and possess fewer chaotic traffic variables than public roads, allowing the startup to refine its sensor fusion algorithms (radar DSP plus vision processing) in real-time operating conditions1. Pre-Series A VC Narrative: The primary strategic benefit of these early deployments is the accumulation of real-world operational data1. DeepGrid can present these active defense and port AGV pilots as working proof-of-concepts to close its requested () Pre-Series A round, demonstrating to investors that its core processor architecture works in real-world tactical environments1. GTM Strategy for ICP Option B: Phased Custom Silicon and Aftermarket Retrofit Volume (Months 6–18) Upon securing the Pre-Series A capital, DeepGrid must initiate the transition to custom silicon while executing a high-volume aftermarket commercial retrofit campaign1. Sovereign Subsidy Leverage via MeitY DLI Scheme: To maximize capital efficiency, DeepGrid must apply to the Design Linked Incentive (DLI) Scheme under the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) implemented by MeitY39.

chunks.section: Tailored Go-To-Market Strategies Mapped to ICP Options
chunks.text: The DLI scheme offers crucial financial support across the semiconductor design and deployment lifecycle40: Product Design Linked Incentive (PDLI): Offers up to reimbursement of eligible chip design expenditure, subject to a cap of per application39. DeepGrid can leverage this to offset EDA tool licensing costs and foundry multi-project wafer (MPW) fabrication fees39. Deployment Linked Incentive: Provides financial incentives ranging from to of net sales turnover over five years, capped at per application, directly subsidizing DeepGrid's volume scaling phase39. Centralized Infrastructure Support: Grants access to the shared EDA Grid and the ChipIN Centre, which provides advanced EDA tools (such as Synopsys and Cadence digital design flows) to supported startups, significantly lowering early design overhead43. Mature Node MPW Fabrication Strategy: DeepGrid must execute its tape-out utilizing a Multi-Project Wafer (MPW) shuttle program on TSMC's mature HPC+ process node, rather than committing to a prohibitive full-mask set costing to 43. An MPW shuttle run shares mask-set costs across multiple startup designs on a single reticle, reducing the entry cost of first-silicon to approximately to for a typical to die area47. This process takes three to six months from GDS-II file submission to physical prototype die delivery43, yielding 40 to 100 fully functional packaged prototype dies for system-level electrical characterization, timing validation, and functional safety verification3. Disruptive Aftermarket Retrofit Distribution: While the custom ASIC is undergoing fabrication and verification in Taiwan, DeepGrid must manufacture and package its homologation-ready ADAS retrofit kits1.

chunks.section: Tailored Go-To-Market Strategies Mapped to ICP Options
chunks.text: Early retrofit units can run on optimized FPGA architectures, transitioning seamlessly to the custom ASIC once first-silicon is verified and delivered1. The target segment is private and truck fleets that must comply with the impending regulatory deadlines1. By pricing its hardware kit at to (representing a massive discount compared to premium imported systems costing upwards of ), DeepGrid can drive rapid, high-volume aftermarket retrofits across thousands of active fleet vehicles1. GTM Strategy for ICP Option C: Tier-1 Component Partnerships and Factory Line-Fit Embedding (Months 18–36) As the custom ASIC transitions from low-volume MPW prototyping to high-volume production at TSMC, DeepGrid must transition from direct aftermarket sales to a scalable, indirect channel model1. Tier-1 Channel Alliances: Early-stage startups cannot survive the multi-year sales cycles, physical supply chain liabilities, and quality assurance processes required by major automotive OEMs1. Consequently, DeepGrid must partner with established domestic Tier-1 auto-component suppliers (such as Uno Minda, Spark Minda, or Bosch India)1. Under this framework, DeepGrid acts as the "Tier-2" technology provider, licensing its custom ASIC and core perception software libraries to the Tier-11. The Tier-1 partner handles physical ECU assembly, system integration, validation testing, and long-term vehicle warranties, piggybacking on their existing relationships with major truck OEMs (such as Tata Motors, Ashok Leyland, and Mahindra) to accelerate market penetration1.

chunks.section: Tailored Go-To-Market Strategies Mapped to ICP Options
chunks.text: OEM Factory Line-Fit Design-Wins: Leveraging the real-world operational safety data gathered from thousands of aftermarket retrofits in Phase 2, DeepGrid and its Tier-1 partners can pitch the custom ASIC directly to commercial vehicle OEMs as a standard, factory-installed component1. By demonstrating that the single-die DGrid Alpha architecture complies with all mandatory local safety regulations at a fraction of the cost of premium imported systems, DeepGrid can secure high-volume, platform-level design wins1. High-Margin Tiered SaaS Subscriptions: Once DeepGrid's hardware is embedded across thousands of fleet vehicles, the startup can activate its recurring SaaS revenue engine, offering tiered subscription packages to fleet managers and transport operators1: Base Compliance Tier (₹10,000 / year per vehicle): Provides basic, real-time safety telematics, automated driver warning logs, and mandatory regulatory compliance reporting for Indian MoRTH and GCC WASL portals1. Advanced Autonomy Tier (₹15,000 / year per vehicle): Unlocks advanced processing capabilities, including real-time driver fatigue monitoring via the H100 bio-ADC and edge-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) visual model analytics1. Premium Autonomy Tier (₹25,000 / year per vehicle): Unlocks advanced Level 2+ collision avoidance, lane keep assist, and adaptive speed compliance parameters delivered via secure Over-The-Air (OTA) updates1.

chunks.section: Quantitative Cost Curves, Unit Economics, and Venture Capital Investment Thesis
chunks.text: To validate its business model to institutional venture capitalists, DeepGrid must show how its custom silicon design translates into structural margin expansion and highly competitive pricing1. Custom Silicon Cost Advantage vs. Foreign Competitors The primary driver of DeepGrid's economic advantage is its complete vertical integration1. Western autonomous computing platforms rely on general-purpose GPUs and CPUs, which require highly complex, multi-chip board configurations featuring separate processors, radar DSPs, CAN controllers, and secure enclaves1. This design drives their compute board BOM to over , forcing these incumbents to target premium, high-margin logistics networks in developed markets to justify the high capital expenditure1. ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ COMPUTE HARDWARE BOM COST ARBITRAGE │ ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ │ │ [ WESTERN INCUMBENTS (Aurora/Kodiak) ] ──────────────► $6,000+ │ │ • General-purpose multi-chip GPU/CPU boards. │ │ • Dependent on advanced 5nm/7nm process nodes. │ │ │ │ [ DEEPGRID SEMI (DGrid Alpha SoC2) ] ────────────────► ~$30 │ │ • Custom, single-die integrated 6-chiplet architecture. │ │ • Fabricated on mature, low-cost TSMC 28nm node. │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Prototyping Cost Analysis and Break-Even Projections Developing custom silicon on a mature node is a highly predictable engineering process3. chunks.section: Actionable Recommendations: The Pre-Series A VC Investment Thesis
chunks.text: For venture capitalists evaluating DeepGrid Semi against global autonomy platforms and domestic semiconductor design startups, the investment thesis is built on three core strategic pillars1: Eliminating the "Hardware Squeeze Zone" via Vertical Integration: Software-only autonomous vehicle startups are structurally squeezed by high third-party hardware costs, as they are forced to purchase expensive merchant silicon compute engines to run their algorithms1. By executing complete vertical integration, designing its own ASIC, integrated radar DSP, and physical compute system, DeepGrid avoids this margin squeeze, capturing both premium hardware margins and high-margin recurring SaaS software revenue1. De-Risking Early Cash-Burn via the Dual-Use Tactical Wedge: DeepGrid is not a pre-revenue startup burning cash while waiting for long-horizon passenger vehicle OEM contracts to mature1. By deploying its currently functional FPGA platforms directly into tactical defense projects and port AGV environments, DeepGrid generates immediate, high-margin contract cash-flow1. This dual-use strategy provides vital operational validation data, cushions the startup's burn rate, and builds physical proof-of-concept traction to de-risk the TSMC tape-out phase1. Capital Efficiency via Sovereign Compliance and Mature Nodes: While foreign incumbents burn hundreds of millions of dollars attempting to design chips on expensive FinFET nodes1, DeepGrid's utilization of TSMC's mature HPC+ node represents an extremely capital-efficient engineering path1.

chunks.section: Actionable Recommendations: The Pre-Series A VC Investment Thesis
chunks.text: Supported by the India Semiconductor Mission's Design Linked Incentive (DLI) Scheme, which subsidizes up to of eligible chip design expenditure and offers sales-linked incentives39, DeepGrid’s requested Pre-Series A round provides a realistic, fully funded path to first-silicon delivery, system validation, and rapid market deployment1. In summary, DeepGrid's GTM strategy intelligently adapts the dual-use pragmatism of Kodiak and the constrained-environment focus of Gatik to the unique regulatory landscape of India and the GCC1. Funding DeepGrid is a calculated bet that aggressive vertical integration on a mature node is the only economically viable method to capture the impending, mandate-driven commercial vehicle safety and autonomy market1.
